[p. 81]

**Sūrat Yā Sīn**

It is also called *al-Qalb* (the Heart), *al-Dāfi'a* (the Repeller), *al-Qāḍiya* (the Fulfiller), and *al-Mu'imma* (the All-Encompassing).

Its purpose is to establish the Message (*al-risāla*), which is the spirit of existence and the heart of all realities, and by which it is sustained. Its benefit is for the one who is sent with it, who is the choicest of the Messengers, and for the Messengers, who are the heart of all existent things, both essences and meanings, to the people of Makkah, the Mother of the Cities, and the heart of the earth. They are the Quraysh, the heart of the Arabs, who are the heart of humankind: with their righteousness, the righteousness of all of them is achieved, and with their corruption, their corruption. For this reason, all the people of the earth gather around them. The greatest benefit of the Message is the establishment of Divine Oneness (*al-waḥdāniyya*), which is the heart of belief, its essence, and its pillar. It is for the Mighty, the Merciful, the Possessor of Majesty and Honour. It is also the warning of the Day of Gathering, which, together with its being hidden from sight, which is one of the special qualities of the heart, is the righteousness of creation. Thus it is the heart of the cosmos, and in it lies the righteousness or corruption of humankind.

The meanings of its names correspond to this: *Yā Sīn*, *al-Qalb*, *al-Dāfi'a*, *al-Qāḍiya*, [p. 82] and *al-Mu'imma*. As for *Yā Sīn*, its explanation will come, regarding how it indicates the secret of the sūra being a heart. It points to the Resurrection, which is among its noblest purposes, by which the heart's righteousness is achieved, and by which the acceptance of what has been mentioned is attained. As for the rest, whoever believes in the Message, it suffices him; it repels from him all his concerns, judges for him every good, and grants him every desire. Each of these [names] has a most complete relation to the heart, as is not hidden.

*Al-Mu'imma* means: the one that encompasses with good and blessing. In *al-Qāmūs* (the dictionary) it is said: "He encompassed them with the gift" (*'ammahum bil-'aṭiyya*), and "He is a bringer of good whose good is all-encompassing" (*mu'imm khayr ya'ummu khayruhu*).

It has thus become clear that this noble sūra, since it is a heart, has in every part of it a profound regard for the heart-ness [of its purpose]:

*Bismillāh* (In the name of God), whose dominion is too exalted to be encompassed by measure. *Al-Raḥmān* (the Most Gracious), who made the warning of the Day of Gathering a universal mercy. *Al-Raḥīm* (the Most Merciful), who illuminated the hearts of His friends with striving for the Day of meeting Him.

Since the heart of each thing is its innermost and most precious part, and since the human heart is hidden from sensation, and since it contains great meanings and hidden and manifest perceptions that become the cause of the body's righteousness or corruption, of its misery or its preservation; and since the Hour belongs to the unseen world, in which the disclosure of affairs occurs and the realities of what is decreed are unveiled; and by attending to it (*mulāḥaẓa*) in the righteousness of its causes eternal happiness is obtained, while by turning away from it and corrupting its causes everlasting wretchedness results: this sūra has explained this in a way not found elsewhere, through the explicit statement placed in its heart, which is its centre, [p. 83] by the blast of death which strikes everyone on earth: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor will they return to their families﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:50], and the blast that resurrects: ﴿And behold, they will rush forth from their graves to their Lord﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:51], and through its explicit statement of the bodily return (*al-ma'ād al-jusmānī*), and its argumentation for it with proof. It is reported that Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī, who was called "the Second Teacher," used to say: "I wish that this divine scholar" (he means the First Teacher, Aristotle) "had come upon this syllogism: God created the bones and gave them life for the first time; and whoever creates something and gives it life for the first time is capable of creating and giving it life a second time. It follows that God is capable of creating the bones and giving them life after their annihilation." Thus this sūra was singled out from the rest of the Qur'ān by this, and it was its heart, as the Prophet ﷺ said, in what al-Tirmidhī narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'ān is Yā Sīn." Abū Ya'lā al-Mawṣilī narrated it, and this is his wording, and so did Imam Aḥmad, in their *Musnads*, from Ma'qil ibn Yasār, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Yā Sīn is the heart of the Qur'ān. No man reads it seeking Allah and the Hereafter except that he is forgiven. Recite it over your dead." [p. 84] Our shaykh, the hāfiẓ (master of hadith) Shihāb al-Dīn al-Būṣayrī, said: "It has a witness from the hadith of Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated by al-Bazzār in his *Musnad*."

This is what Allah guided me to, and to Him belongs praise, regarding the explanation of the secret of its being a heart.

Then I saw that al-Burhān al-Nasafī said in his *Tafsīr*, which is an abridgement of the great *Tafsīr* of Imam al-Rāzī, at the end of the sūra, after mentioning the hadith: "al-Ghazālī said regarding it: this (i.e., its being a heart) is because faith is valid only with the acknowledgment of the Gathering (*al-ḥashr*), and the Gathering is established in this sūra in the most eloquent manner, so it was made the heart of the Qur'ān for this reason." Imam Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, the meticulous and verifying scholar, approved of it. It may also be said: this sūra contains nothing but the establishment of the three principles: Oneness, Prophethood (*al-risāla*), and the Gathering, with the strongest proofs. It begins with the explanation of Prophethood, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the Messengers﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:3]; its proof is what He placed before it in His saying: ﴿By the Wise Qur'ān﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:2]; and what He reported about it in His saying: ﴿So that you may warn a people﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:6]. It ends with the explanation of Oneness and the Gathering in His saying: ﴿So glory be to Him in whose hand is the dominion of all things﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:83], an indication of Oneness; and His saying: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:83], an indication of the Gathering. [p. 85] There is nothing in this sūra except these three principles and their proofs. Whoever attains this much of the Qur'ān has attained the portion of his heart, which is assent (*taṣdīq*) that is in the heart (*al-janān*). As for what is in the tongue and what is in the limbs, that is in other sūras. Since this sūra contains only the works of the heart, it was named "the Heart." For this reason it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that it was recited at the head of one approaching death, because at that time the tongue is weak in strength and the outward limbs have lost their power, but the heart has turned to Allah and withdrawn from everything else. So there is recited at his head what increases strength in his heart and strengthens his assent to the three principles." End of quotation. There is some alteration in the text.

As for his statement, "The function of the tongue and the limbs is not present in this sūra at all," it may be contradicted by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And why should I not worship Him who created me?﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:22]; ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you"﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:47]; and ﴿And that you worship Me; this is the straight path﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:61].

The hadith he mentioned was narrated by Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā'ī, Ibn Māja, Ibn Ḥibbān, and al-Ḥākim, from Ma'qil ibn Yasār, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet: "Recite Yā Sīn over your dead." Ibn al-Qaṭṭān regarded it as defective (*a'allahu*), and al-Dāraquṭnī graded it weak. The author of *al-Firdaws* attributed (with a chain) from Abū al-Dardā' and Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "No dead person dies and Yā Sīn is recited beside him except that Allah makes it easy for him [p. 86] ." It was narrated by Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Ḥibbān in *Faḍā'il al-Qur'ān*, from Abū Dharr alone, may Allah be pleased with him. Aḥmad in his *Musnad* narrated from Ṣafwān ibn 'Amr, who said: "The elders used to say: when Yā Sīn is recited beside the dying person, it is lightened for him by it." Ibn Ḥibbān said: "The intended one is the one at the point of death (*al-muḥtaḍar*)."

From this explicit statement of the Gathering there draws its support everything scattered in the Qur'ān concerning mention of the Hereafter, by whose observance and mastery there is the righteousness of all conditions in both abodes, and by whose neglect and forgetting there is their corruption in both. This is in addition to what it shares with the other sūras, in that it gathers all their meanings found in *al-Fātiḥa*: the Most Beautiful Names, *Allāh*, *al-Rabb* (the Lord), *al-Raḥmān*, *al-Raḥīm*, *Māliki Yawm al-Dīn* (Master of the Day of Judgement), "He in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned"; the command to worship by following the straight path; the distinction of the people of bliss and the people of hellfire; and the establishment of the three principles by which the accountable person becomes a believer: Oneness, the Gathering, and Prophethood, which is the heart of existence and by which its righteousness is achieved. It is a sustainer for every spirit by which a pleasant life is attained. It is the starting point of righteousness, just as the Resurrection is its final goal. The seal of these is the human being, the very eye and heart of existent things. So it established this in the clearest and most emphatic manner. [p. 87]

Together with what the sūra opens with, the disconnected letters placed at its beginning, serving as a pillar of the Qur'ān and a sharpener of minds, for the two categories of the dotted and the undotted, and the two qualities of the voiced (*majhūra*) and the whispered (*mahmūsa*).

Since the heart of a human being is the principal object of the cosmos, and lies about a third of the body from the head; and since the letter *yā'* among the letters of *Abjad* is at about that position (it is the tenth of them), and the letter *sīn* is at that location among the letters *a b t th* (it is the twelfth of them); and since these two letters, with what they contain of voicing, rise above the extreme of weakness, and descend, through what they have of whispering, from the extreme of hardness: this is an indication that the sound heart is the glassy, transparent one, combining firmness and softness. It rises by its firmness above the softness of water, in which no image remains; and descends by its delicacy from the hardness of stone, on which almost nothing is impressed except with the utmost effort. So it combined firmness and softness, prepared to receive images impressed upon it that remain, so that it would be receptive and beneficial. It would thus be a repository of attributes originated by power and choice, which are indicated by the sūra of *al-Malā'ika* (the Angels); and by knowledge of good, so that it would attract it, and of evil, so that it would avoid it. Thus there would be within it a witness from itself to the true belief concerning its Maker.

The voiced letter is stronger, so *yā'* was given precedence for its voicing. The two letters, despite their difference in voicing and whispering, agree in being open (*infitāḥ*), soft (*rakhāwa*), and low-placed (*istifāl*). This is an indication that the heart is not fit, as already mentioned, with firmness (which is in the sense of voicing) except through humility (*ikhbāt*), which is in the sense of whispering; and through descending from the extreme of firmness to the limit of softness, so that it is not stony and hard; by being open, so that it is beneficial and receptive; and by being low-placed, so that through its humility it reaches its Lord.

The *sīn* gained in sibilance (*ṣafīr*), which contains intensity, spread, and strength, to compensate for its weakness compared to *yā'* in whispering, so the two became equal. Its sibilance indicates the blast in the Trumpet, which this sūra explicitly states. The voicing of *yā'* indicates its strength. That it is one of the letters of calling (*ḥurūf al-nidā'*) indicates its going beyond limit in intensity, until from it there appear those effects that empty the abodes, that expel the young and the old, and then that overtake them from every quarter, in compliance with the command of the One, the Subduer.

Their point of articulation is from the tongue, which is the heart of the three points of articulation, because it is central and because its benefits in this are many. *Yā'* is from its middle, and *sīn* from its tip. These two points, despite being central, are the pivot of most letters. In addition, there are secrets in them that are too subtle to be conceived by thought.

Allah (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Yā Sīn﴾. If the meaning is "O human being," then it is the heart of all created existents, [p. 89] their essence, their secret, and their kernel. If it is intended as "O master," then it is the choicest of those who lead them. If it is intended as "O man," then it is the choicest of humankind. If it is intended as "O Muḥammad," then it is the choicest of men, who are the kernel of humankind, who are the secret of the living, who are the very essence of existents. Thus it is the choicest of the choicest, the elite and the essence of the heart.

It seems that whoever said its meaning is "Muḥammad" looked at the agreement of his name ﷺ in the value of letters (*jummal*, numerical reckoning), taking the right-hand letters of the doubled consonant, and the numerical value of "qalb" (heart), and the value of the names of the two letters. It is not hidden that the hamza in the name of *yā'* is a second alif. So the total of its value is twelve.

Since the proof of the Messenger's prophethood ﷺ was established in the earlier discussion of "the angels," and his people were warned against turning away from him, and since his Sender (Exalted is He) is All-Seeing of His servants and All-Knowing of what sets them right, and of who among them is fit for prophethood and for other things, and since the root meaning of the verb "qara'a" (to recite; to read) – as has passed in the commentary on Surat al-Hijr – is gathering together, along with distinction; and since that is the highest station of those travelling toward God, and it is the function of the heart, he expressed it in the oath with His words: ﴿And the Qur'an﴾; and described it with the attribute of the knowing heart, saying: ﴿the Wise﴾. That is: the one that combines indication of knowledge, adorned with action, and guidance toward action, made firm by knowledge.

Since it was established in the surah of "The Angels" (Sūrat al-Malā'ika, Surah 35) that He, glory be to Him, is the Supreme King, owing to the perfection of His power that was established for Him and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge; and since among the most excellent fruits of kingship is the sending of messengers to the subjects by the commands of the King, and their turning away from what they are upon, which the souls have called them to and which their desires and appetites have led them to, toward what He opens for them of generosity and what He makes them see of wisdoms; and since prophethood (al-risāla) is one of the three foundations that move a person from disbelief to faith, and it is the one looked to first, because it is the cause of the other two foundations; and since they had rejected His message out of aversion and arrogance, He said, presenting it (al-risāla) before its effect, by way of emphatic affirmation together with the pronoun of address, which admits no ambiguity:

﴿Indeed, you are surely among the messengers﴾; that is, those whose intellects have governed the promptings of their souls, so that they became—by the luminous power that Allah bestowed upon them—like the angels, whom He mentioned in the previous surah as His messengers; and they are counted among them by what they have adopted of His commands, His prohibitions, and all that He is pleased with.

The Prophets, peace be upon them, are from his light (ﷺ), because he was the first of them in creation and the last of them in being sent. In reality they were only paving the way for his law. Allah, glory be to Him, sent him only to perfect noble character. Among noble qualities, Allah made it so that he would speak to people only in ways their minds can bear. The number of the messengers, as in the hadith of Abu Umamah al-Bahili from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in Ahmad's *Musnad*, is three hundred and fifteen, and in it the number of the prophets is one hundred and twenty-four thousand. It is also in al-Tabarani's *al-Kabir*, from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned only the number of the messengers. Before faith, the minds of the Arabs could in no way accept that they were from him. So Allah, glory be to Him, swore openly that he is from them, and symbolically, inwardly, pointed to the fact that they are from him, by making the number of the letters of the names of his name "Muhammad" (ﷺ), which He indicated by the two letters at the beginning of the surah, equal to their number. It is as if He said: "Indeed you, O Yasin, whose interpretation is (Muhammad), whose letters' names add up to their number, are from their origin." Thus it became a symbol within a symbol, a precious treasure within a treasure, a secret within a secret, and a righteousness leading to righteousness. It is sweeter in the intimate conversation of beloveds than explicit address.

Then He attached to the passive participle His saying: ﴿on a path﴾, meaning a wide, clear road; ﴿straight﴾, meaning: you are among those who have been established as being upon it. It is the most complete straight path, which was mentioned earlier in al-Fatihah, because it belongs to the special ones upon whom favour has been bestowed. And because of His saying (exalted is He) concerning Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both: ﴿And We guided them both to the straight path﴾ [al-Saffat: 118]. Thus its tanwin, in accordance with what the oath and the emphasis point to, is for magnification. The meaning is that this great attribute has been established for them, and you are one of them, by sharing with them in the proofs. So no one has the right to single you out from among them for denial.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When Surat Saba' and Surat Fatir clarified the greatness of His dominion (exalted is He), His unity in that, His singularity in that dominion, creation and origination, such that minds fall short of conceiving even its lowest degree, and one encompasses none of it except what He wills; and they indicated, through proofs and signs, what removes doubts and clarifies the way, concerning what thoughts had grown dull in grasping, and heedlessness had overcome, so that they seemed to have frozen from their accustomed movement, He, glory be to Him, reminded them of the blessing of stirring them, so that they might reflect on it by praising Him for choosing the one whom He chose to explain those signs and selected to clarify those evident truths. So He said (exalted is He): ﴿Ya Sin﴾ [Ya Sin: 1], ﴿By the wise Qur'an﴾ [Ya Sin: 2], ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya Sin: 3], ﴿upon a straight path﴾. Then He said: ﴿That you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾ [Ya Sin: 6]. Thus He pointed to what the blessing of warning produces, and what awakening through reminder stirs. Then He mentioned the cause of those who remained blind after being stirred, even if it is attributed to a seal upon the heart and to an evil predestination: ﴿The word has certainly come into effect upon most of them﴾ [Ya Sin: 7], and so on. Then He indicated afterward that some of those who were blinded at first sight to the greatness of those proofs may be moved, at the stirring, by their earlier happiness. So He said (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, We bring the dead to life﴾ [Ya Sin: 12], meaning: so We do with these people when We will to guide them. ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. Then He mentioned the custom of the obstinate and the way of the deniers, along with the explanation of the matter, saying: ﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town﴾ [Ya Sin: 13], and so on. He followed this, glory be to Him, with the clear evidences and proofs He placed in existence, saying: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [Ya Sin: 31], the verse. Then He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have brought it to life﴾ [Ya Sin: 33], up to His saying: ﴿Will they not be grateful?﴾ [Ya Sin: 35]. Then He said: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya Sin: 37], ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Ya Sin: 40]. Then He said: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾ [Ya Sin: 41], up to His saying: ﴿for a time﴾ [Ya Sin: 44]. Then He mentioned their aversion despite the greatness of these proofs, their denial, their evil state at their resurrection, their regret, their rebuke, and the testimony of their limbs against their deeds. Then the verses wove together, flowing in a way that suits what came before, to the end of the surah. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 5:

Since it was as if it had been said, "What is this that he has been sent with?", it was as if it had been said, in answer to the one who asked: it is the Qur'an, the very thing by which the oath was sworn, and it is ﴿a revelation (tanzil)﴾; or, in the sense of ﴿a revelation of the Mighty﴾, that is, the One characterized by all attributes of perfection. Since this attribute (al-'Aziz) pertains to subjugation and dominance, and that would not be an attribute of perfection except when joined with mercy, He said: ﴿the Merciful﴾, that is, the One who encompasses all attributes of generosity, who bestows favor upon whomever He wills of His servants after having bestowed the favor of bringing them into existence, by establishing them upon the path (minhaj) that He is pleased with for them. He is the One who has no like at all, by reason of the might with which He subdues and the mercy with which He restores.

﴿He sent it down to you﴾, while it is in the sublimity of its composition (jalalat al-nazm), the eloquence of its speech (jazalat al-qawl), the sweetness of its casting (halawat al-sabk), the strength of its construction (quwwat al-tarkib), the solidity of its arrangement (rasanat al-wad'), the wisdom of its meanings (hakim al-ma'ani), and the soundness of its structures (ihkam al-mabani), at the highest peaks of inimitability (i'jaz). He made its revelation gradual according to what is beneficial, in a correspondence (mutabaqa) that rendered creation incapable of producing its like. Then He arranged it in an order other than the order of its revelation, an arrangement that made creatures incapable of grasping all that is intended from the seas of its meanings and the wisdom of its structures. So all of it is inimitability, with whatever it contains of expansion (itnab) and conciseness (ijaz).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 6:

When he mentioned the one sent (al-mursal), the message sent (al-mursal bihi), and the one who sends (al-mursil), he mentioned the one to whom he was sent (al-mursal lahu). So He said: ﴿That you may warn a people﴾; i.e., people possessed of strength, power, intelligence, and perspicacity. ﴿Whose fathers were not warned﴾; i.e., they were never warned at all. ﴿Their fathers﴾; i.e., those who altered the religion of their greatest forefather, Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and those who came after them during the period of interval between the messengers (fatra al-rusul). Since the absence of warning necessitates that desires and appetites take control over the intellect, so that heedlessness of the path of salvation results, He said: ﴿so they are heedless﴾; i.e., because of the period of interval. Or the meaning, on the view that "ma" is a second object of "li-tundhira": that you may warn them with what their fathers were warned of, those who lived before the alteration; for these people are heedless of that because of the lapse of time and the occurrence of forgetfulness.

Since prolonged residence in something produces familiarity with it, and familiarity is destructive of what it necessitates, namely persistence in what one is accustomed to, because of love for it: "Your love for a thing blinds you and deafens you." He said, in answer to one who anticipates the answer concerning what their condition has produced: ﴿The word has certainly come into effect﴾; that is, the complete [judgment] in its domain, which is the necessitating of punishment, through constant heedlessness; ﴿upon most of them, so they do not believe﴾; that is, because of that; ﴿they do not believe﴾; that is, in what is conveyed to them of warning; rather it increases them in blindness and arrogance on earth, and in the evil of scheming.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on Surah 36, verse 8:

Since the meaning is that no new faith arises among them after the clear proof and the dazzling wisdom, and since this is a strange matter, he explained it by what it entails of depicting their state, to portray His might, exalted is He, and the brilliance of His greatness, to which the speech turned in order to make it understood. What has been mentioned is, today, a meaning and an example, and in the Hereafter it will be an evident reality. This condition had never left them and had not ceased. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We have placed﴾, that is, by the greatness We possess; He emphasised it because of their denial. ﴿Chains upon their necks﴾, that is, from the darknesses of error; each neck is shackled. By the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) He indicated that, because of their narrowness, the chains pressed the flesh until it folded over the iron, so that it nearly covered it; thus the neck, with it in it, became as if it were inside them, while they encircle it.

Since it is known that when iron is placed on the neck its weight drags it down to the shoulder, He did not mention the direction of downward descent but mentioned the direction of elevation. So He said: ﴿so they are﴾, that is, the chains, by their width, reaching by means of this placement ﴿up to the chins﴾, plural of *dhaqan* (ذَقَن), which is the meeting point of the two jaws. Therefore they prevent the head from bowing. Since this raising of the head is the act of the arrogant, and since their arrogance was in a place not befitting it, He (exalted is He) made clear that they are compelled to it; it is therefore humiliation within, though it appears as pride without. So He said: ﴿they are﴾, that is, by reason of this reaching, ﴿raising their heads (*muqmahun*)﴾, from *uqmiha al-rajulu* (أُقْمِحَ الرَّجُلُ), when another made him *qamih*, that is, made him one who raises his head, lowers his gaze, and looks only with part of his sight, in the posture of the arrogant. Its root is from the saying *qamaha al-ba'iru* (قَمَحَ البَعِيرُ), when the camel raised its head while drinking and did not drink the water. In combining *al-'Ubab* and *al-Muhkam* [two lexicons], he said: Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said, describing the ship of one of them (Abu Hayyan said: the corpse of one of them) which he would bury:

*"And we sat upon its sides, lowering our glances like thirsty camels that refuse water."*

Al-Razi said, in *al-Lawami'*: *al-muqmah* is one whose head is pulled back to his back, in the posture of a camel. Al-Qazzaz said: *al-muqmah* is one who stares fixedly with his eyes, raising his head. Abu 'Amr said: *al-qamih* among camels is the one that does not drink while being very thirsty, and whose self does not accept water. *Al-qamh* is the verbal noun of *qamahtu al-shay'* (قَمَحْتُ الشَّيْءَ), and *al-iqtimah* is your taking a thing in your palm and then tossing it into your mouth, that is, swallowing it; its noun is *al-qumhah*, like *al-luqmah* and *al-akhlah*. End of quotation. It seems that the *muqmah* is from this, because his posture at this swallowing is the raising of the head and lowering of the gaze, or fixing of the gaze when swallowing is difficult for him; and God knows best.

Thus this is an image of their raising their heads away from looking at the one who calls, out of arrogance and haughtiness, to the extent that if they were able to inhabit the air they would not hold back, out of obstinacy and bewilderment. Or it is because they abandon this great, good matter, worthy of being turned toward and drunk from, while they are in the utmost need of it. In that state they are like the thirsty camel that refuses water despite its intense thirst; what prevents it is a great obstacle that has made it raise its head, but its matter is hidden, so it does not know what it is. For this reason He formed the verb in the passive, indicating that they are compelled to forfeit their share of this sublime matter.

Since the one who raises his head is not prevented from looking ahead of him, He said: ﴿And We have placed﴾; that is, by Our greatness. And since the intent was to bar them from a particular good, namely that which leads to complete felicity, and not from everything that benefits them, He introduced the preposition and said: ﴿before them﴾; that is, the direction that is possible for them to know, ﴿a barrier﴾. And since when a person's one direction is blocked he turns to another, He said: ﴿and behind them﴾ (p-98), that is, the direction that is hidden from them. He repeated the barrier to emphasize their denial of that and to confirm His making it; so He said: ﴿a barrier﴾; that is, every direction they turn to has become blocked, so they are unable to look at the truth or to reach it. Therefore He said: ﴿So We have covered them﴾; that is, We placed upon their sight, by the greatness We possess, a covering; ﴿so they﴾; that is, because of that; ﴿do not see﴾; that is, this description does not renew for them the seeing of the truth, and no benefit comes to them with outward sight or inward insight at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 10:

When they were deprived by this of the sense of sight, he informed about the sense of hearing, and so said: ﴿And it is alike﴾; that is, equal, and balanced to the utmost degree of balance, without any kind of difference. He added to the indication of their lack of intellect by using the particle of elevation (ʿalā, "upon"), as a notification that if they refuse when warned by one who is above them, they will be even more stubborn with others. So He said: ﴿upon them, whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾; that is, whether we have informed you of it, of the admonitions that prevent disbelief, or not. ﴿They will not believe.﴾ Then he clarified that what their condition stood equal in, through what the covering (ighshāʾ) had caused, is the absence of faith; so he said, resuming the statement: ﴿They do not believe.﴾

(p-٩٩) When he had explained what was the preventing cause that kept them from seeing, it became known that the preventing cause from hearing is similar to it, because the One who informs is Mighty. So whenever He does something, it is in a manner in which no stratagem is possible. And when He informed that the majority are of this description, the listener yearned (istishraf) for a sign by which the few who are saved could be known, because they are the intended party in essence. So He said, in answer to that: ﴿You can only warn﴾; that is, a warning from which the one warned benefits, so that salvation results from it. The meaning is: only he believes by your warning ﴿whoever follows the Reminder﴾; that is, who exerts himself in following everything that reminds of God from the Qur'an and other than it, through which its possessor is mentioned and honoured; ﴿and fears the All-Merciful﴾; that is, fears the One whose mercy is all-encompassing, with a great fear. The turning of the speech away from the aspect of majesty to the description of being the All-Merciful indicates that for the people of fear, reminder of beneficence suffices them for admonition. ﴿in the unseen﴾; that is, because of what is reported to them of His unseen powers, especially the Resurrection, whose exclusive matter in its ultimate clarification is because it is a matter of heart, without seeking a manifest sign that removes the veil, such that the matter becomes one of witnessing with no unseen in it. Rather, it is an allowance for what is permissible of His vengeance, even by cutting off His beneficence, because of what has been established for Him in the Surah of "Fatir" of power and choice. And he fears Him also with sincere fear, in the state of his being absent from those among the people who would show off to him. These are the ones whom the warning benefits, and they are the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), of whom it was established in "al-Baqarah" that the Book is a guidance for them, while for others there is no path to its being upright. ﴿Do not let yourself perish in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], for upon you is only the warning; indeed God is Knowing of what they do. Whoever God knows has this fear, He draws him near; and whoever He knows has hardness, He turns him back upon his heels, by the covering that stands between him and it. And God is the Granter of success.

When the context indicated that this one benefited himself, the listener yearned to know his reward. So He said, making the pronoun singular in accordance with the sequence already established, observing the wording of "man" (whoever), indicating the scarcity of this category of people among all of them in this all-encompassing Surah, by its being a heart, as opposed to what is scattered in other places: ﴿so give him good news﴾; that is, by reason of his fear in the unseen; ﴿of forgiveness﴾; that is, for his sins, however great they are and however often he commits them and repents of them, for that does not prevent the attribute of fear. And when knowledge of the erasure of sins was attained, both their essence and their effect, He said: ﴿and a generous reward﴾; that is, lasting, great, wholesome, delightful, continuous, with no turbidity in it in any way.

When he had explained the second principle, which is the Messengership, and followed it with its fruit, sealed with good tidings, and when the third principle of faith, which is the Resurrection, was a great cause for ascending to belief in the Oneness (tawhid), which is the first principle, and when most of those who fear Him, glorified is He, were restricted in their worldly life, with their lives embittered, He gave the reason for these good tidings, to make known that this reward in this abode is through the inner garments, which are splendid, of knowledge, tranquility, blessings and peace of heart, and after the Resurrection through the outer garments, which are radiant and which are caused by the inner worldly garments, which are hidden, not for their own people. [This was] as good tidings for them and as a warning for the group before them. He said, introducing the Resurrection, because of what was mentioned of its benefit, turning the speech to the locus of majesty, as a notice of the greatness of these purposes, and that none protects these sincere ones, despite their fewness and their being distinct from the earlier ones, despite their multitude, except He who has the overwhelming majesty:

﴿Indeed We, it is We,﴾ meaning: by what We have of majesty, which cannot be matched; ﴿give life to the dead﴾, meaning: gradually now, and all at once at the Hour; ﴿the dead﴾, meaning: all of them, physically through resurrection, and in meaning through deliverance, when We will, from the darkness of ignorance; ﴿and We write﴾, meaning: of good and other than it, one thing after another, so that the detail does not exceed anything in that summary; ﴿what they sent before﴾, meaning: of all their deeds, states and words, collectively, at the blowing of the Spirit; ﴿and their traces﴾, meaning: their sunnahs (ways) which remain after them, whether good or not good; and We recompense each according to what he deserves in the Last Abode, in which the recompense does not cease. So there is no nobler than Him, if He is Generous.

Since that might give the impression of being limited to writing down what was mentioned of the states of the children of Adam, or of the need for writing, he indicated His power over what no power can be exercised upon by anyone other than Him, in the smallest little of what was mentioned; so how about what is above it? So he said, in the accusative (nasban), as a conjunction of a verbal sentence upon a verbal sentence, which is ﴿We write﴾:

﴿And everything﴾, meaning: of the affairs of the living and others; ﴿We have enumerated it﴾, meaning: before its existence, by Our eternal knowledge, as enumeration; and We have recorded it ﴿in a clear imam﴾, meaning: a book worthy of being referred to, ﴿clear﴾, meaning: in which nothing of all the states is hidden from anyone who wishes to know it from it. So to Allah belongs this overwhelming power, the manifest majesty and the dominating might. Thus the verse is of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which each of two parts omits what the other mentions): the act of enumeration indicates its source, and the mention of the imam indicates the act of writing.

When the discourse reached this point, and the purpose of the surah was, as has passed, the establishment of the Messengership, for warning of the Day of Gathering, and the warning was an end, and ends are the purposes in themselves, and the end of the warning was following the Reminder, that was the end of the end. The discourse about the followers was more deserving of precedence, although speech about them necessarily entails speech about their opposites, who are those who turn away, against whom the Word has been justified, and speech about the Day warned of. Therefore he struck the comprehensive parable that encompasses all of that, and proceeded to (p-103) depict the Resurrection with a depiction not preceded by its like. Then he joined, with the verse of the effacing (of faces) and what follows it, to the group that turns away. Then he returned to speech about the Messenger and the Book.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 13:

When He, glorified is He, had indicated His complete power through awe-inspiring acts, both of the sensory and of the non-sensory kinds of death and life, both in beginning and in return, and since striking parables with observable things is the thing most closely attached to the mind, most decisive in ending dispute and contention, and most revealing of the states that are intended, He said, linking it by conjunction to "so give them good news" (fa-bashshirhu), explaining the third principle, which is the first in essence, the primary aim in itself, namely monotheism (al-tawhid), while joining to it the other two principles so that the parable may be comprehensive and the proof through it clear and radiant: ﴿And strike for them﴾, that is, on their account, a parable of good tidings of what is hoped for them when they turn toward (the truth), and warning of what is feared for them when they turn away and retreat; ﴿a parable﴾, that is, an observable one, in their persistence in opposing the Messenger, and his patience with them and his gentleness toward them. For We sealed their hearts upon disbelief, despite their nearness to you in lineage and dwelling, and the success of others, for We illuminated their hearts despite distance in lineage and dwelling, with faith and its fine fruits, because they fear the Merciful unseen and do not persist in heedlessness and doubt.

When He mentioned the parable, He substituted for it His saying: ﴿the people of the town﴾, which is the place of wisdom, the gathering of the word, the spreading of knowledge, and the source of mercy. Since the thing used as the parable is in reality only the report of its people's states, because the town is the point of resemblance, and its reports were many over lengthy periods, He specified the intended matter by His saying: ﴿when﴾, which is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the town," stripped of its adverbial (zarfiyyah) sense. Since one who comes to a region of a city, even if it is large, is customarily considered to have come to that city, He returned the pronoun to the place of the message, to confirm it and to express in definition the extent of the remoteness of the farthest point, so He said: ﴿there came to it﴾, that is, to the town, to warn its people; ﴿the messengers﴾, that is, from God, since they were from His messenger Jesus, peace be upon him, whom He sent by His command, to establish what pleases Him, glorified is He, and to negate what He dislikes; they are among those of whom it was said in (Surat) Fatir: they came with the clear proofs and with the scriptures. The definiteness is either because they know the town and know its affair, or because it is very famous, so that if they asked anyone among the People of the Book, who take care of it, he would inform them of it, since it is well known that they used to refer to them with questions, so that they might clarify for them, as they claimed, the points of difficulty.

Since the Prophet ﷺ's greatest concern in this context was to console him over their hesitation to hasten to belief in him, despite his calling them with the Wise Book to the Straight Path, and since sharing in calamities is the greatest consolation, He substituted for His words "when it came to them" a detailed explanation of that coming. He said, attributing it to Himself (p-105) the Holy, because that is greater in consolation: ﴿When We sent﴾. That is, by the greatness that belongs to Us. Since the intended object of the message was its bearers, He said: ﴿to them two﴾. That is, so that each of them would strengthen the other, making their matter more forceful. They informed them of their being sent to them, as if they had said: "We are messengers to you, so that you may believe in God." ﴿But they denied them both﴾. That is, despite the signs they had. For it is known that We never sent a messenger without his having with him signs of the kind on account of which mankind believed, whether he came directly from Us without an intermediary, or through Our messenger, as happened to al-Tufayl ibn 'Amr al-Dawsi, Dhu al-Nur (the Possessor of the Light), when he went to his people and asked the Prophet ﷺ that he might have a sign. It became a light on his forehead. Then he asked that it be somewhere other than his face, and it became on his whip.

Since mutual support in a matter makes it stronger in its standing and more helpful toward what is intended from it, He stated as a consequence of that His words, omitting the object because it is understood from the context, and because the intended aim is to show power over bringing about the act and directing it toward whatever is willed for it: ﴿then We strengthened﴾. That is, We brought about 'izzah (might), which is strength, vigor and dominance, for Our command or for Our messenger, on account of the weakness that had befallen them through being denied. Thus what We willed of might was achieved, by what the recitation of Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, pointed to, with the lighter reading (in the qira'ah, the canonical recitation) ﴿with a third﴾, (p-106) whom We sent with what We had sent the two of them with. ﴿Then they said﴾. That is, the three, after they came to them and their insistence on denial had become evident to them, emphasizing according to what they saw of their denial: ﴿Indeed we are sent to you﴾. That is, not to anyone else. ﴿Sent﴾.

They said: "You are nothing but mortals like us." That is, the people of the town said: "You are not [anything], [even if your number has increased]; except—" and when the exception negated the negation, the doubt of what had been attached was removed, so its effect was removed, and his statement "a mortal like us" was put in the nominative. That is: what is the particular distinction you have over us that you should be messengers rather than us?

Since the sense of the phrasing was: "You have been sent to us with nothing," they followed it with their statement: "Nor has the Most Merciful revealed anything." That is: the All-Merciful; His mercy being general, together with our equality in His servanthood, requires that He treat us equally in mercy, so He does not single you out with anything over us. And they went to the extreme in negation with their words: "anything [min shay'in]."

Since the coming [of messengers] in the manner mentioned is open to the possibility of error and the like, they said, rejecting that: "[In]" (that is, "not"); "you are only lying," that is, in state and in outcome.

"They said": that is, the messengers said: "Our Lord": that is, He who, even if we had no restraint from lying about Him except His kindness toward us, would be sufficient; "knows": that is, and for this reason He manifests the signs through our hands and protects us from those who plot against us. This expression is treated as an oath, and similarly ﴿Allah bears witness﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. And when they confronted them with this denial, emphasized to the utmost, they added emphasis to their reply, saying: ﴿Indeed, we are sent to you﴾; that is, specifically; ﴿certainly sent﴾; we did not come to you by mistake, nor with a lie. The first is the beginning of an announcement, and these two are replies to denial; so He gave each its due.

(p-107) When they had established this among themselves, they followed it with its proof, and with the announcement that the consequence of denial does not reach them with any harm, as a way of pointing them to the warning of the Mighty King's punishment. So they said: ﴿And upon us is nothing but the clear delivery﴾; that is, as an obligation, from the One who sent us, who is Allah (Exalted is He), to whom belongs all command. ﴿But the clear delivery﴾; that is, the one supported by decisive proofs, from the arguments that are verbal and practical, by miracles and other things. Were it not that He knows, none of that would have been possible for us. Just as your gods, since they have no knowledge, could not make any clear statement about their affair, so too, since the knowledge of our Sender concerning our messengership is established, He is the Witness for us in what manifests at our hands, and sufficient is He as a Witness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 18:

When the dwelling of the righteous among people sometimes becomes a blessing and at other times a curse, depending on whether they are believed or denied, and whether they are treated well or ill, then those who denied these messengers were afflicted, because of their denial of them, with trials such as the barrenness of the land, the hardship of the times, and similar tests. He (Allah) mentioned what effect this had on the people of the town, so He said: ﴿They said﴾. And since they saw in the messengers signs and manifest marvels, which bore witness to their blessing and the auspiciousness of their company, such that when they insulted them they expected the people to deny them, they emphasized their statement: ﴿Indeed, we see an omen in you﴾; that is, we burdened ourselves with taking omens and bad augury, a manifest taking of omens, as indicated by the explicit mention, (p-108) unlike what is in "al-Naml" and "al-A'raf". ﴿In you﴾: by attributing the affliction that befell us to your ill omen, because it is the habit of the ignorant to take omen by what they incline toward, and to ascribe to it whatever blessing befalls them, and to take omen by what they dislike, and to ascribe to its ill omen whatever calamity strikes them. Then they began anew, as a conclusion (istinaf al-nata'ij), with their statement, by way of emphasis, to inform that what they reported has no interruption, even though people like them seem improbable to the wise: ﴿If you do not desist﴾; that is, from this your calling; ﴿we will surely stone you﴾; that is, we will surely revile you, or we will pelt you with stones, until you desist; or we will surely kill you in the worst manner of killing. And since a person may do something whose effect is not taken, they said, expressing it with the verb "touch" (massa) rather than "touch harmfully" (imsas): ﴿And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us﴾; that is, promptly, and not from anyone else, just as you threaten us with what will befall us from the One who sent you; ﴿a painful punishment﴾, until you desist from us, so that we may refrain from causing you pain.

﴿They said﴾; i.e., the Messengers; ﴿your omen is with you﴾; i.e., your ill omen, which brought affliction upon you; ﴿with you﴾; that is, your ugly deeds, of which your denial is one.

Since nothing had appeared from them except what, on sound consideration, calls for good fortune and blessing, namely reminding you of God, in whose hand is all good, they rejected your divining ill omen from them, clearly showing that there is no cause for it other than what they had shown. So they said: ﴿Is it because you have been reminded [of God] that you take omens from us?﴾ i.e., is it because a reminder of God has come to you that you have taken an omen from us? Since that could not in any way be a cause for divining ill omen, they turned away from it, alerting them that the locus of the ill omen is their excess and nothing else. So they said: ﴿Rather﴾; i.e., the matter is not as you claim, that the reminder is a cause of divining; rather ﴿you are a people﴾; i.e., what God gave you of strength to carry out what you wish has deceived you; ﴿who are wasteful﴾; i.e., your habit is to go beyond the limits and to transgress, so you were punished for that.

When the context established that the matter is in the hand of God, so there is no guide for whom He leads astray and no misleader for whom He guides, He guides the distant in place and lineage when He wills, and He leads astray the near in both when He wills. Since distance of abode is usually tied to distance of lineage, al-Biqa'i placed the place of coming before its doer, to make clear that the call benefited the farthest and did not benefit the nearest. So he said: ﴿And there came from the farthest end of the city﴾; i.e., the most distant. This is unlike what preceded in Surat al-Qasas. For this same purpose he departed from the expression "the town" (qarya), as previously mentioned, and said: ﴿the city﴾, because it is more indicative of greatness, which entails distance of its extremities and the gathering of mixed peoples. When he specified the doer by saying ﴿a man﴾, he showed his concern for forbidding the evil and his eagerness to remove it, as is obligatory, by saying ﴿running﴾; i.e., he hastens in his walk, faster than walking but short of running, out of eagerness for the sincere counsel of his people.

When the soul yearned for the one calling to his coming, his statement ﴿He said﴾ clarified him. He won their sympathy by saying ﴿O my people﴾, and commanded them to strive against their souls by saying ﴿Follow the messengers﴾; i.e., in worshipping God alone, and in everything they command you.

Then he drew their attention to what calls them to follow the messengers and what prevents them from turning away from them, by saying, repeating the verb to show the intensity of his concern with it: ﴿Follow﴾, that is, with the utmost of your effort; ﴿those who do not ask you﴾, that is, in any state whatsoever; ﴿for a reward﴾. And since he used the singular pronoun, taking into account the wording "man" (whoever), to indicate the obligation to follow whoever possesses this quality which indicates the messengership, even though it refers to one person, he used the plural, to make clear the priority by means of mutual support, cooperation, agreement in purity, and distance from defilement, which indicates the unity of purpose that indicates the necessity of truthfulness; so he said: ﴿and they are guided﴾, that is, guidance is established for them and does not part from them; whatever they intend, they never fail to hit the right aim of what is correct. So you will succeed through the religion, which necessitates success in the Hereafter, and nothing of the world will escape you. Thus he gathered the comprehensive elements of encouragement in this concise statement.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 22:

When the context made clear that he had said: "Indeed I have followed them in the worship of Allah," he built upon it his statement, as a reply to those who blame him for that, as an encouragement toward what he had chosen for himself, and as a rebuke to those who refuse it: (p-111) ﴿And why﴾; that is, and what reason is there for me ﴿not to worship He who originated me﴾; that is, and to Him I shall return; so to Him belongs my origin and my return. And what is the matter with you that you do not worship He who originated you, ﴿and to Him﴾; that is, not to anyone else, ﴿you will be returned﴾ likewise? So He deserves to be worshipped: in gratitude for what He bestowed at the beginning, and out of fear of His consequence at the end. The verse is thus of the type known as ihtibak (the omission of a corresponding element from each of two parts): the phrase "and to Him I shall return" is omitted at the first mention, because of what is indicated by its second mention; and his denial directed at them is mentioned at the second, by means of what is indicated at the first, namely his denial directed at himself. This is done to win them over by displaying fairness and avoiding explicit mention of opposition. In it there is also an admonition to them regarding what makes gratitude obligatory, and a warning against committing disbelief.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 23:

When he had explicitly commanded and implicitly forbidden, encouraged and warned, rebuked and reproached, and made clear the greatness of those who believed in Him and of those who were the cause of that, he denounced those who did otherwise by denouncing themselves, belittling those whom they worshipped besides God while they were immersed in His blessings. So he said, indicating by the form of the verb (ifti'al) that in this there is opposition to the original nature (al-fitrah al-ula): ﴿Shall I take﴾; and he made clear the exaltedness of His rank, glory be to Him, by his saying: ﴿besides Him﴾, that is, equal to Him, despite the lowness of their station; and he made clear the powerlessness of what they worshipped by its plurality, so he said: ﴿gods﴾. Then he confirmed that by his saying, showing by the particle of doubt (in) that benefit is greater than harm, as an encouragement toward Him, glory be to Him: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills harm for me﴾, a light will, indicated by the omission of the yā' (in yurid-ni), or a strong will, indicated by its affirmation; manifest, indicated by its vowelling; or hidden, indicated by its being sukun (unvowelled).

When he had reminded them of His originating him, glory be to Him, as guidance that they are likewise, he stated explicitly what encompasses them, saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, that is, the one whose blessing is general over every creature, of the worshipper and the worshipped. He warned them by his saying: ﴿harm﴾, and he nullified the most far-reaching of what they believe about them by his saying: ﴿their intercession will avail me nothing﴾, that is, nor will it avail anyone like me in this; ﴿their intercession﴾, that is, even if it were supposed that they interceded; but their intercession would not produce ﴿anything﴾ of benefit.

When the singular "intercession" indicated that they are counted as nothing, even if their intercession and cooperation were united at a single moment, he indicated by the plural pronoun that they are likewise, whether they are gathered together or scattered, saying: ﴿nor can they rescue me﴾, that is, from his calamity, should the matter lead to opposition to what He has willed; for by the mere act of His will, what He wills comes to be. A weak rescue, indicated by the one who omitted the yā', nor a strong one, indicated by the one who affirmed it; manifest, or hidden;

Then he began, with various kinds of emphasis, to state what follows from the conduct of sensible people who give sincere counsel to themselves. He said this emphatically, because of their denial of him, by not turning back from their objects of worship: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in clear error.﴾ That is: if I were to take those (gods) — ﴿then indeed I would be in clear error﴾ — that is, encompassing me, such that I could not attain any kind of guidance with it; ﴿clear﴾ — that is, evident in itself to whoever is not enveloped by it, making clear to every observer the darkness that he is in.

Having established the proofs, and no one who opposed him retaining any excuse, he declared openly what he had hinted at of his faith. He said, displaying his joy through emphasis and cutting off what they might suppose, that he would not dare to break with all of them by opposing them in the foundation of the religion: ﴿Indeed I have believed﴾; that is, I have brought about the assent (tasdiq), which in reality is no assent other than this, in the Messengers, believing them, lest I introduce into their affair some kind of confusion, whether denial or otherwise. And when he had guided them by hinting at the all-encompassing Mercy, he declared to them what it is incumbent upon them to thank Him for, namely the specific Lordship, and he said: ﴿in your Lord﴾; that is, by means of the One from whom there is no bounty with you except from Him. You have forgotten what He has for you of Lordship, Mercy, and originating (al-ibda'). He increased his plainness with them, showing his indifference to them, by his saying: ﴿So hear me﴾; that is, hear, if you wish, so that you may take heed, or if you wish, you may conceal it, by what the deletion of the ya' (ي) and its affirmation indicate. So do not say after that: "We did not hear him; and had we heard him we would have done with him such-and-such." Then they rushed at him in a single rush, as one man, and killed him. The Prophet ﷺ had informed that the likeness of the companion of "Ya-Sin," this one, in this Community is ʿUrwa ibn Masʿud al-Thaqafi, when he called his people to Islam and proclaimed his adherence to it with the adhan, and they shot him with arrows and killed him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 26:

Since it is known, from the hardness they showed in denying the messengers and threatening them, together with the signs they had, that they would not spare this one (the man who came from the farthest part of the city), and since he had openly told them that if they overlooked him, most of their affair would fall apart for them, He (Exalted is He) did not mention it, counting it among what need not be mentioned. And He said, (p-114), in answer to one who longed to know the state of this man after that, with His saying, briefly in exposition and encouraging the people of faith:

﴿It was said﴾; that is, to him, after they killed him. He built the verb in the passive and omitted the agent, because the intended matter is the saying itself, not the one who said it, and the one addressed is known. ﴿Enter Paradise﴾; because he was a martyr, and the martyrs roam in Paradise wherever they wish from the moment of death.

Since the human nature inclines to love vengeance against one who has done harm, He (glory be to Him) explained that the chosen ones are not in that state. So He said, resuming the narrative: ﴿He said: "Would that my people knew"﴾; that is, those among whom there is strength for what is required of them. For if their strength had been against the disbelievers, it would have been good; ﴿knew﴾;

When he wished to state explicitly that the favour had been bestowed upon him, he resolved the verbal noun into his saying: ﴿with what My Lord forgave me﴾; that is, He caused concealment to fall over what I had been committing throughout my life of disbelief in Him, through faith within a brief period; ﴿My Lord﴾; that is, the One who was good to me in the Hereafter, after His goodness in this world; ﴿and made me﴾. Since companionship is the greatest success, he turned away from saying "honoured" to his saying: ﴿among the honoured﴾; that is, among those whom He gave the lofty ranks, because they spent all their lives in worship. So he gave counsel to his people, both living and dead, wishing that they might know of Allah's (Exalted is He) honouring of him, so that they would act as he acted and attain what he attained. In his story there is an exhortation to hasten to abandon the wicked and to follow the righteous, to show forbearance toward the ignorant, to restrain anger, to be gentle in rescuing the wrongdoer from his wrongdoing, and that no one enters Paradise except by the mercy of Allah, even if he is a doer of good. This is like what occurred with the Ansar (the Helpers) - may Allah be pleased with them - in hastening to faith despite the distance of their homeland and lineage. Also in the words of those among them who were martyred at "Bi'r Ma'unah" (the Well of Ma'unah), as narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Campaigns, from Anas - may Allah be pleased with him: "Convey to our people that we have met our Lord, and He is pleased with us and has made us pleased." And at the Battle of "Uhud", as in the biography (al-Sirah) and other works, when they found the goodness of their food and drink and the excellence of their resting place, they said: "Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us, lest they become indifferent to jihad and shrink from war." So Allah (Blessed and Exalted) said: (I will convey it to them on your behalf). Then Allah (Exalted) revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169] and the verses following, in the Surah of "Al 'Imran". In citing this story there is an indication that among the Quraysh are those who will end their lives in disbelief, and the term allotted to them will not be cut short; He (glorified is He) supports this religion through others, so that His power may be manifest, and so that those (others) may complete their appointed terms; then He turns the hearts of others toward it, so that His wisdom may be manifest along with that. And beyond this are other springs of meanings and firm foundations of structure.

When He, glory be to Him, had made most of the armies of this noble Prophet angels, and had strengthened him with them in both situations, peace and battle, and had guarded him from those who wished him harm in the honoured city of Makkah and after leaving it, He reminded him of this by His words, linking (ʿāṭifan) them to what is implied (taqdīruhu) in the following: "We did not send down upon his people, before they killed him, any army from the heaven that would intervene between them and that, as We did with you, when Abu Jahl intended to kill you with the rock while you were prostrating at the House, and others (intended) other than that, which is detailed in the biographical works (al-Siyar). As for after the Hijrah (migration), (it was) at the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), when We sent against them a wind and armies that turned them back defeated, and at (the battles of) Uhud, Badr, and Hunayn, and other than these." The verse: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾, with Our majesty; ﴿upon his people﴾, that is, the companions of Yasin (Ya-Sin); ﴿after him﴾, that is, after his killing; and he intensified the negation with His words ﴿any army﴾, and he affirmed the intended meaning with His words ﴿from the heaven﴾, that is, to destroy them; and he affirmed that sending heavenly armies is a matter specific to the Prophet ﷺ, because it serves wisdoms that return to victory without total annihilation (istiʾṣāl), for they appear in the forms of human beings and perform their actions. As for the punishment of total annihilation, the divine custom (al-sunnah al-ilāhiyyah) has held that it does not occur with more than one angel, because that is more indicative of power. Therefore He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We were not going to send down﴾, that is: that was not of Our custom, nor was it valid in Our wisdom that the punishment of total annihilation should come by a large army.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 29:

﴿In it was only a single cry﴾; that is, nothing; ﴿it was﴾; that is, the event by which they were punished; ﴿only a single cry﴾; Jibril (peace be upon him) cried it at them, and they all died, to the last one. He emphasized its matter and established its singleness by his saying ﴿single﴾; that is, because of the insignificance of their affair in Our sight. Then he increased their belittlement by explaining the speed of their destruction in his saying ﴿and behold, they were extinguished﴾; that is, extinction is established for them, as though they had never had any movement at any time of the ages. (p. 117) Among the fine verses on this is the saying of Abu al-'Ala' Ahmad ibn Sulayman al-Ma'arri:

Life is like fire: its ashes are from its end and its beginning is smoke.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 30:

When He (subhanahu) had informed them of the truth of their situation, encouraged them with the parable He had set forth for them, and warned them, and this did not benefit them, it produced regret over them, and over those who were likened to them and those who resembled them. So He (ta'ala) said: ﴿O anguish﴾; i.e., this state deserves the lasting presence of a great anguish, ﴿upon the servants﴾. It is as if it were said to it: Come, for this is one of your states in which you ought to be present, since these people are worthy that one should grieve over them. Ḥasra (anguish) is the intensity of regret over what has passed, whose loss burns and whose matter is beyond remedy, so there is no way to reverse it. It is also possible that the meaning is that, because of the abundance of their wrongdoings, the causes of anguish never leave them, and nothing else is present with them; so they have no companion except it, and no one overcomes them or prevails over them except it.

Since it was as if it were said, "What state?", He said, explaining it and giving the reason for the grief by mentioning its cause: ﴿There does not come to them﴾, and He emphasized the negation and generality by His saying: ﴿any messenger﴾, i.e., whichever messenger it was, at whatever time it was, ﴿but they used to mock him﴾; i.e., they used to produce mockery toward that messenger. Yet the messengers are the furthest of creation from mockery in state, speech and deed; and it is clear that one who mocks someone of such a state is ruined, so he deserves to have anguish constantly attached to him and to be grieved over.

(p. 118) When He, glory be to Him, had completed the account of the first state of those who were made examples of, and the first and last state of the believer among them, this lament indicated that the destruction of the deniers is a matter that must occur. He pointed to it by expressing wonder at their failure to consider their own selves, by threatening the listeners among them, and by warning them of the final outcome of those made examples of, in a manner that encompasses all the past nations and the bygone groups, through His words: ﴿Have they not seen﴾; that is, let these people whom you invite know, with a knowledge that is like sight, through the reports that are authentic to them and the traces they have witnessed, ﴿how many We have destroyed﴾, by virtue of the greatness that is Ours. His words ﴿before them﴾, being an adverbial of place without the preposition being mentioned, indicate that what is meant is the entire span of time that preceded them, from Adam until their own time. The inclusion of the preposition with those destroyed indicates that what is meant is some of them. The result of all this returns to the meaning: Look at all that has passed of time: has any people been punished in it with the punishment of total annihilation except because of their disobedience to the messengers? So He said: ﴿of generations﴾; that is, the many, the mighty, the great. "Qarn" (generation): al-Baghawi said, the people of each era, so named because of their being associated in existence. ﴿that they﴾; that is, because the generations. Since what is meant by "rasul" (messenger) is not one particular individual, and since the form "fa'ūl," like "fa'īl," is one in which the masculine, the feminine, the singular and the plural are alike, He returned the pronoun to the whole, so He said: ﴿to them﴾; that is, to the messengers specifically, insofar as they are messengers; ﴿do not return﴾; that is, from their corrupt doctrines, and they single out the messengers for following, so they do not follow anyone else at all in any matter, whether religious or worldly. Thus Our practice is consistent, and you will not find any change in Our practice: whenever a people denies their messenger, We destroy them and save their messenger and those who follow him. Do these people not fear that We will subject them to that same ancient and upright practice? Here "that" (anna) is causal, on the understanding that the particle of cause has been omitted, as is well known in many places. The pronoun in "that they" refers to the people addressed by the messengers, and the pronoun in "to them" refers to the messengers. No one with sound taste and a upright disposition doubts this. The expression in the present tense serves to indicate their being given respite, the patience shown toward them, and forbearance concerning them, together with their persistence in obstinacy through the renewal of not returning. "Return" here is like His words (exalted is He): ﴿And We will surely make them taste of the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, that perhaps they may return﴾ [al-Sajdah: 21]; that is, return from their corrupt ways. This is without doubt the meaning of the verse, and the statement of one who said that the meaning is that the destroyed do not return to the world, so as to convey a refutation of those who believe in the return (raj'ah, return to worldly life), is not sound, because the Arabs are not among those who hold that belief; and even if it were granted, it would not be fitting, because the context does not support it, since nothing had preceded from them except mockery, so He denounced their mockery, (p. 119) while knowing that God (exalted is He) has established His practice that whoever mocks the messengers and opposes their word, and does not return to it, He destroys him. This practice is consistent and has not failed in any nation, as happened to the people of Noah, Hud, and those after them. None of them was exempt, and the Arabs know their histories and look upon their traces. Likewise they know the story of Moses, peace be upon him, with Pharaoh. So the context is one of threat, and the meaning becomes: Have these people not seen the multitude of those We destroyed from among those before them because they opposed the messengers? Then do they not fear the like of that in opposing their messenger? This accords with the reading with the kasra (qirāʾah al-kasr, the reading of "inna" with a kasra), which al-Burhan al-Safaqusi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and others, from al-Hasan. They said that it is a resumptive clause, so it is as if on the assumption of someone asking: Why did He destroy them? This is like when it becomes widely known that a certain valley has not been traversed by anyone without being struck; this would be a deterrent from traversing it, and if someone intended to do so, it would be correct to say to him: Do you not see that no one has traversed it without perishing? That would be a warning to him and a restraint from persisting in it, because the cause of the destruction is only its traversal. That is more effective in restraining him than saying to him: Do you not see that people die, and that many of them have died, and none of them has returned? Without attributing that to anything of traversing the valley or anything else, for this is a matter known to him, not conveying any new benefit. The fact that they do not return to the world likewise has no bearing on causation, because that is known to those addressed; rather (p. 120) they even assert something greater than that, namely that there is no life after death, neither in this world nor in another. Even if it were granted, mentioning the return of the dead would more fittingly be a threat, for each person among them then returns to what is in another's hand, of what he had died possessing, and the one who was followed becomes a follower; or war occurs and strife arises. Thus it is clear that the threat by the non-return is not fitting. And God is the One who grants success in what is correct.

When many people of ignorance, and those of zeal and pride, do not care about destruction in pursuing their desires, relying on the belief that one brief death in a moment is easier than forcing the soul to do what it does not want, so that they would have deaths at every moment, He (Exalted is He) informed that the matter is not ended by worldly destruction. Rather, there is disgrace, humiliation, abasement, punishment, and pain that never ends. So He said: ﴿And indeed, all of them﴾; that is, indeed they, all of them, not one of them is excepted. He added emphasis to increase the denial of them with His saying: ﴿lamma﴾. Whoever reads "lamma" with a shaddah (tashdid, doubling of the letter mim), the meaning according to him is: "and not all of them except that." He indicated that they come humbled and compelled when they are all gathered together at the place of standing, with no one to help them and no one to prevent them, and none of them is absent, in any state of staying away from being overcome. So He said: ﴿all gathered﴾. He indicated the strangeness of the condition in which they are gathered with His saying: ﴿before Us﴾, and He increased the magnitude by making it manifest in its appearance. He expressed it with the active participle derived from the passive form, comprehensive, considering the meaning of "kull" (all), because it is more indicative of gathering at one time, and it is more indicative of greatness: ﴿brought forth﴾; that is, on the Day of Resurrection, after their being raised in their own persons, just as they were in the world, equally. This indicates that this gathering is against their will, and that it is a matter that is established, binding, and permanent, as though, because of its great firmness, it has never ceased, and that there is no escape from it and no way to evade it, and that it is easy, requiring no pause except the permission. When permission is given, every one who is commanded by it among the soldiers does it, whoever he may be. How excellent is what the poet said:

Had we, when we die, been left alone, death would be a rest for every living being.
But when we die, we are raised, and after it we are questioned about every thing.

When he had completed the parable that demonstrates the completeness of His power over the awesome acts, through good tidings and warning, so that whoever God has sealed upon his heart does not believe, even if he is close in kinship and dwelling, while whoever has placed fear in his heart believes, even if his lineage and place of visitation are far from him, the definition was complete with the category that is intended in itself, namely the one who follows the Reminder (al-dhikr). He concluded with the resurrection, and they were deniers of it. He had placed it at the beginning of the discourse as part of the completion of the good tidings for those who follow the Reminder. He indicated this with His words, beginning with an indefinite noun whose tanwin (nunation) indicates its magnification: ﴿And a sign﴾, that is, a great indication, ﴿for them﴾, of Our power over resurrection and Our bringing it into existence. ﴿The earth﴾, that is, this kind of thing of which they are part. Then He described it with what realized the aspect of resemblance, saying: ﴿dead﴾, which has no life, because there is no plant in it, whether or not there was once a plant in it that perished, crumbled, and became dust, or there was never anything in it at all. Then He resumed explaining that it is a sign, with His words: ﴿We have brought it to life﴾, that is, by originating plant growth in it, or by restoring it, through the cause of rain, as it was after its decay.

Since bringing forth the staple foods is another blessing, He said: ﴿And We bring forth from it grain﴾. He (exalted is He) drew attention to the great power in it and to the generality of its benefit by the mode of majesty, and He increased the admonition by reminding that grain is the principal sustenance of living beings. So He said, placing the prepositional phrase (al-jār) first, indicating that other things are considered as nonexistent in comparison to it because of its great impact and the generality of its benefit, as evidenced by the fact that whenever it becomes scarce, famine comes and harm occurs: ﴿from it﴾, that is, by means of this bringing forth, ﴿they eat﴾, that is, it is truly grain. They know this with ʿilm al-yaqīn (knowledge of certainty), ʿayn al-yaqīn (the certainty of sight), and ḥaqq al-yaqīn (the truth of certainty), and they cannot claim in any way that this is a magical illusion.

In this verse and similar ones there is a great incitement to reflect upon the Qur'an and to extract from it the meanings that indicate the majesty and perfection of God. Here Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri, may God have mercy on him, recited, in his tafsir (exegesis), in censure of one who neglects this, and he said:

Oh you who sits in the seat of leadership
in the issues of jurisprudence, dictating and teaching,

You have been heedless of the proofs of monotheism, which govern it;
you have built a branch, but you have not laid the foundation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 34:

When He - glorified is He - had mentioned what is in the crops, and what has no stem, of blessing and power, and the context indicated restriction in it, He followed it with what shows that the intended meaning is magnification, not true restriction, by manifesting the favour in other things, from the great trees and the small ones, which bear foods and fruits. So He said, indicating its greatness through the mode of majesty: ﴿And We have made﴾; i.e., by what We have of majesty; ﴿in it﴾; i.e., in the earth; ﴿gardens﴾; i.e., orchards, which conceal what is within them by the intertwined trees in them.
