And since the palm tree, together with the benefit in it, is always an adornment, in that its leaves do not fall, He placed it first and named it by its name, so He said: (p-125) ﴿of palm trees﴾. There is also in it an indication that it is entirely benefit: its wood, its fibre, its branches, its fronds, its bunches, and its fruit, in the form of spathes, heart of the palm (jummar), unripe dates (busr), ripe dates (rutab), and dried dates (tamr). For this reason - and God knows best - it came in it with the plural form of abundance (jam' al-kathrah), like ﴿al-'uyun﴾ (the springs). And since the vine does not have an adornment with leaves that cover, except while the grape is still present, He said: ﴿and vines﴾. By the plural in both of them, and not in the grain, He indicated the great variety of kinds within the single type, which necessitates the apparent difference in quantity, taste, and other things.

And since the gardens are not fit except with water, and it is in the nature of water to sink into the earth and settle with the intensity of its flow downward, its gushing upward was a striking matter to the intellect, which does not happen except by the compulsion of a wise compeller. He said: ﴿And We caused to gush forth﴾; i.e., We opened great openings; ﴿in it﴾; and this indicates the extremity of His greatness and its exaltation above being encompassed by any part of it, by the partitive with His saying: ﴿springs﴾. The definite article here indicates that the earth is constructed upon water, so every place in it is suitable for water to gush forth from it; but God restrains it from some places, unlike the trees, of which none generally covers the earth. In that there is a reminder of the blessing in withholding water from some of the earth, so that it may be a place of dwelling; and had He willed, He would have caused the earth to gush forth springs, as He did with the people of Noah - peace be upon him - so He drowned the whole earth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 35:

(p-126) Since the life of every thing is only through water, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾. The reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, with the plural form alongside the singular pronoun, indicates that a single tree gathers, by grafting, various kinds of fruit. ﴿Its fruit﴾ means: of the fruit of what has been mentioned before. Had there been no water, it would not have sprouted, and had it not been in abundance, it would not have borne fruit after sprouting.

Since a human may play a part in raising some things, He, glorified is He, negated the causes in that which one might claim as a cause, and drew attention to the fact that all of it is by His creation. So He said: ﴿and their hands did not make it﴾, meaning: they did not produce any of that, ﴿their hands﴾, meaning: by weak labour. What is indicated by the feminine form of the verb is this; so how about what is greater than it? Even if they joined forces in that, as indicated by the plural of "yad" (hand). Since the context is clear on this, the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim came with the pronoun omitted, not intended, restricting the verb, generalising the object, and referring all matters back to their Originator, whether they were by means of a cause or without a cause. That is: their hands had no work in any of the things, neither in this nor in anything else that has a part in their livelihood or from other than it. For this reason, His rebuke to them for their lack of gratitude is most fitting, by His saying: ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾, meaning: they should persistently and always offer thanks, and continually renew it at every moment, on account of these great blessings.

Since the context aims to establish the Oneness of God, and to inform that what is worshipped besides Him has no entitlement to worship in any respect, no power to benefit, and no power to harm, and since this context produces, through what it indicates of His singularity in every perfection and that no one shares any command with Him in any way, His transcendence (tanzih) above the association they claimed, to the utmost degree, He said, turning the speech away from the manifestation of majesty because establishing it through mercy, which indicates it, is more effective in exalting Him: ﴿Glory be to the One who﴾. He described Him with what confirms what came before: the attribution of all affairs to Him, and the negation of any part of them from anyone else. So He said: ﴿created the pairs﴾, meaning the kinds that resemble one another yet differ in attributes, in tastes, in fragrances, in shapes, in forms, in natures, and in other matters that none can count except Allah. These indicate, in the greatest indication, the perfection of power, the magnificence of wisdom, and freedom of choice in will. He emphasized with His saying ﴿all of them﴾ to convey generality. Then He made the matter clearer in explanation by His saying ﴿of what the earth grows﴾, so every plant, tree, mineral, and other thing that is generated from it is included. He pointed out, since this is in the context of their denial, to their discipline, by belittling them through the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah, the grammatical form for small numbers) and by the expression "selves" (anfus), which is generally used for what is disparaged: ﴿and of themselves﴾. He made clear that behind that are matters that none knows but Him, glory be to Him, so He said: ﴿and of what they do not know﴾, meaning of what they do not need in their religion or their worldly life, and on which the rectification of livelihood and of the Hereafter does not depend. Had that been the case, He would have informed them of it, just as He informed them of the conditions of the Hereafter and other things we did not know.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 37:

When He had trained them to reflect upon the signs in perceptible objects, which indicate the overwhelming power [of God], especially regarding resurrection, He elevated them to abstract meanings in that same manner. For the bringing into existence of each of the two worlds (al-malawayn, i.e., the two realms of the upper and lower world), after its annihilation, is the most evident proof of resurrection. So He said, transferring them from the universal place to the universal time, which combines both substances (jawahir) and accidents (a'rad): ﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾; that is, as proof of the restoration of a thing after its passing away; ﴿the night﴾; that is, which they witness, about which there is no doubt among them, and for which there is no means in any way of removing it. Then He resumed His saying: ﴿We strip off﴾, returning to the locus of greatness (mazhar al-azamah), as an indication of the sublimity of this act in particular.

Since the original state of this existence is darkness, and light is something that occurs (hadith), and since its light is not pure, He expressed it with "min" (from), which is suitable for accompaniment (mulabasah) together with penetration into the parts (takhallul fi al-ajza'), so He said: ﴿from it the day﴾; that is, which had been mixed with it; by the removal of the light and the unveiling of it from the true reality of the night; ﴿then behold, they﴾; after Our removal of the day which We had stripped from the night; ﴿are in darkness﴾; that is, they enter into darkness, by the appearance of the night which the light had been covering, as the skin covers the sheep. Al-Mawardi said: This is because the light of the day penetrates into the air, so it brightens; when it departs from it, it grows dark. Ibn al-Jawzi transmitted it from him. The context has definitively indicated that the implied meaning is: "And the day, from which We strip off the night which had been its covering and dominant over it; then they are seeing."

When he had mentioned the two times, he mentioned their two signs, saying: ﴿And the sun﴾, meaning the one from which the day is stripped off from the night by its setting. ﴿Runs﴾. Since its setting at night is like a person's resting in his lodging, and its being placed on a course that was measured for its movement each day, by a measure without deviation and a path that does not bend, He said: ﴿for a fixed course﴾, meaning a great one, ﴿for it﴾, which is its movement that it does not exceed to the south or to the north, going and returning, while it is swift within it. This is shown by the expression with the particle *li* (for) in place of *ila* (to), and the reading "there is no resting place for it" supports this. Rather, it is always running until the end of the world, in a firm, established place, one fit for rest. He expressed it this way even though it does not come to rest as long as this existence lasts, so that it would not be imagined that the continuance of its motion is because the place of its running cannot be settled upon. This is not contradicted by what is in Sahih al-Bukhari (Sahih al-Bukhari) and in the Book of Faith of Sahih Muslim (Sahih Muslim), from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Its fixed place is beneath the Throne. It goes and asks permission to prostrate, and permission is granted to it. It is as though it has been said to it: 'Return from where you came,' and so it rises from its west." This is the wording of Muslim, and the wording of al-Bukhari will come. It is possible that the fixed course is the last of its running, at the annihilation of this existence. (p-١٣٠)

Since this running follows an order that does not fail over the passing of years and the succession of ages, the imaginations grow weary of extracting it, and the understandings are bewildered in deducing it, so He magnified it by saying: ﴿That﴾, meaning the matter that dazzles minds. He increased its greatness with the intensive verbal form (*taf'il*) in His saying: ﴿the measure﴾. He confirmed this, turning the speech away from the general manifestation of greatness to restricting it to the two attributes of might and knowledge, to exalt this verse and to alert that it is the greatest of the signs of the heaven. So He said: ﴿the Mighty﴾, meaning the One whom no one can overpower in any part of His affair, and He is dominant over everything. ﴿the Knowing﴾, meaning the One who encompasses everything in knowledge, who manages the affair so that it proceeds in a wondrous order and a marvelous method, which never weakens and never suffers any kind of disorder at any time, until He, glorified be He, wills the annihilation of this universe, and its motions cease and its existing things perish. Al-Bukhari related from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the mosque at sunset, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where it goes?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes until it prostrates beneath the Throne, and it asks permission, and permission is granted to it. It is about to prostrate, but it will not be accepted from it, and it will ask permission but it will not be granted to it. It will be said to it: Return from where you came. That is His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And the sun runs for a fixed course for it﴾.'"

When he mentioned the sign of the day, he followed it with the sign of the night, saying: ﴿And the moon﴾. Its meaning in the recitation (qira'a) of Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Rawh from Ya'qub, with the nominative (raf'), is: "it runs toward a station of its own." The rest read it in the accusative (nasb), which indicates the greatness of this running, because of its speed: it covers in a month what the sun covers in a year. For this reason he made the verb that explains the governing particle (nasib) weaker and made it operate on the pronoun referring to "the moon," so that the moon would be mentioned twice, which indicates intense concern and draws attention to the magnitude of the action concerning it. He repeated the expression of greatness and said, beginning a new clause in the nominative reading: ﴿We have determined it﴾. That is, we measured it with a great measure; that is, we measured its course ﴿as stations﴾, twenty-eight of them. Then it hides for two nights at the conjunction, and for one night at the waning, and it cannot exceed them by a day. Al-Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said: It moves away from the sun and keeps receding until it returns as a full moon (badr); then it draws near, so that the more it approaches the sun, the more it diminishes in itself, until it vanishes. ﴿Until it returned﴾; that is, after it had been a great full moon, ﴿like the old palm-stalk (\'urjun)﴾ of the date palm. The \'urjun is the stalk of the cluster (\'idhq), from its branches (shamarikh) down to its end, where it is attached to the palm tree, being thin and curved. It is of the pattern "fu'lul," and the lexicographers mention it under the letter nun, and they say: "\'arjana al-thawb," meaning he decorated the garment with designs resembling the stalks of dates. The exegetes said that it is derived from "\'arija," meaning it became crooked. Since its redness tends toward yellow, he said ﴿the old﴾ (al-qadim), that is, the one that has changed. When the \'urjun remains for a long time, it becomes like this: thin, bent, and yellowed.

When it was established that each of the two has stations it does not overstep, so that what is the sign of one does not overpower what is the sign of the other, but rather, when the authority of this one comes, that one departs, and when that one comes, this one departs, and when the two come together the Hour is established, the conclusion of these premises became clear: ﴿Nor is it for the sun to overtake the moon﴾; that is, the sun, which is the sign of the day; ﴿it is not for it to be possible﴾; that is, so long as this existence remains in this order; ﴿to overtake﴾; that is, because its movement is slow; ﴿the moon﴾; that is, so that it would obliterate it entirely. Thus the day does not outrun the night, ﴿nor does the night outrun the day﴾; that is, so that it would be possible for the moon, despite the speed of its course, to overtake the sun and overpower it, so that no day would exist at all. Had it said "yastabiq" (contend in racing), the meaning would have been disturbed, because it would give the impression that one does not precede the other at all. So the verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which something is omitted from each of two parallel clauses, each part supplying what is missing from the other): it first negated the sun's overtaking of the moon, on account of its strength, as evidence for what was omitted from the second clause, namely the negation of the moon's overtaking of the sun; and it mentioned second the night's outrunning of the day, on account of the strength it has (p-133) through what intervenes of the day, so that it covers it, as evidence for the omission of the day's outrunning of the night first. ﴿And each﴾; that is, of those mentioned, in reality and in metaphor; ﴿in an orbit﴾ encompassing it. Since He ascribed to them the actions of rational beings, and since they follow a fixed order that does not fail, and a determined course that does not deviate or cease, He was exalted above any blemish that could befall it or any weariness that could reach it, and He expressed it with what its root meaning revolves around: power, intensity and expansiveness. So He said, bringing the plural pronoun of rational beings because it is more indicative of their being constantly subjugated: ﴿they swim﴾; as an incitement to reflect upon the signs in them which the ignorant, through their great familiarity with them, have neglected.

When he had mentioned the limits He set for swimming upon the face of the sky, such that if one transgressed them the order would be disrupted, he mentioned what He prepared of ships for sailing upon the surface of the water, the ship that covered the earth in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, until it was like the sky. Had the ship exceeded the limits He, Exalted is He, set for it of stations, it would have passed through into the Sea of Darkness, and the matter would have been ruined. They would have been in it as if they were on land, and by its movement as if they were cleaving mountains, deserts and wastelands. All of this is a reminder of the Days of Allah, an alert to the abundance of His blessings, a warning against His assaults and His retribution, and a favour upon them by what He facilitated for them of traveling the sea and reaching great benefits through it. So He said: ﴿And a sign for them﴾, that is, [p. 134] a sign of Our complete power and Our all-encompassing knowledge; ﴿that We﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness; ﴿carried﴾. Since those before Noah, peace be upon him, from the origins of mankind were not carried in the ship, he turned from the expression by the pronoun and the fathers to His saying: ﴿their offspring﴾, that is, the offspring of mankind, whom We created (dhara'a), scattered (dharawa) and multiplied (dharara) until We filled the earth with them from that time until the end of time. Because of this multiplicity understood from this eloquent derivation, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and the Kufans preferred the singular reading, while the reading of the rest with the plural (jam') added clarity, some of them visibly and some of them in the loins of their fathers. ﴿In the ship﴾: he made it definite because of its fame among all people. ﴿The laden﴾, that is, the loaded, filled with animals and provisions, while it moved upon those waters, the like of which had never been seen nor will ever be seen. Yet despite that, Allah delivered it safely.

When this verse did not stop, but rather He—glorified is He—generalized its benefit, He said: ﴿And We have created﴾; that is, by Our overwhelming majesty; ﴿for them of the like of it﴾; that is, of the like of that ship; of the camels and the ships; ﴿that which they ride﴾; that is, continuing upon that on a basis of renewal, so that they may pursue their benefits; and if We willed, We would have prevented that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 43:

Since He, glorified is He, had delivered our forefathers when He carried them in that water, which was unlike any other ever was, and since they might have thought that the deliverance was due to some secret among the secrets, other than His will, He made the matter of what He created from its like sometimes, and sometimes so that it would be known that this was by His craftsmanship, so that His blessing would be thanked first and last. Thus He said: ﴿And if We will﴾; that is, by virtue of the all-encompassing power that We possess; ﴿We drown them﴾; that is, although this water on which they ride is not able to reach (the depth of) that which We carried in it, their forefathers; ﴿then there is no one to cry out for them﴾; that is, no helper who would rescue them from the drowning that We intend for them; ﴿nor are they saved﴾; that is, by themselves, without a helper; ﴿they are rescued﴾; that is, there would be for them a rescue; that is, deliverance by themselves or by others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 44:

Since He, glory be to Him, grants aid (yuṣrikh) to whomever He wills, so that He rescues them, and since "lā" (no) is a negation that encompasses everything (nafyan mustaghriqan), He made an exception for what comes from Him, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿Except as a mercy﴾; that is, except that We, so that We rescue them if We will; as a mercy ﴿from Us﴾; that is, for them; not as an obligation upon Us, nor for a benefit returning to Us from them; ﴿and an enjoyment﴾; that is, for them; ﴿for a time﴾; that is, and it is the time of the end of their appointed terms.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 45:

Since this state was known to them, they do not dispute it in any way; rather, when they fall into it, they sincerely make supplication, call upon Him alone, and cast off the rivals (al-andad). The knowledge of this should compel its possessor not to be heedless of the One who is able to do this at any time; indeed, he should not slacken in thanking Him, out of fear of His scheme (makr). When a sensible person is reminded of a matter and knows it with certainty, he is worthy of accepting it; but if he does not accept it, and is warned of its consequence through something merely possible, he strives earnestly to guard against it. He (Allah, glorified is He) marvels at their turning away from Him, despite the presence of decisive proofs of His oneness, and that He is able to do what He wills of punishment and reward, and at their turning toward what does not benefit them in any way. So He said: ﴿And when it is said﴾, i.e., by whatever speaker it may be, ﴿to them: Be wary﴾, i.e., fear with a great fear, through which you exert effort upon yourselves, ﴿of what is before you﴾, i.e., of the deadly stumbles into which you may fall, in both abodes; ﴿and what is behind you﴾, i.e., what you have neglected and not been requited for, and of which there must be accounting, because God, who created you, is the Most Wise of judges; ﴿that you may be shown mercy﴾, i.e., that you may be treated with the treatment of one who is shown mercy through honor.

Given that the sense is: "They turn away, because turning away has become a habit for them; they cannot free themselves from its grip," he follows it with his words, drawing attention to this: ﴿And there never comes to them﴾; he generalises with his words ﴿any sign﴾; he specifies with his words ﴿of the signs﴾; and he turns the speech to a reminder of favour, as a refutation of them in their claim that they are the most thankful of people to the Benefactor. So he says ﴿of their Lord﴾, i.e., the One who does good to them; ﴿but they turn away from it﴾, i.e., despite its coming from the One whose kindness has overwhelmed them and whose bounty and grace have encompassed them; ﴿constantly﴾, i.e., their turning away is continuous.

When mercy in provision and victory is attained only through showing mercy to the weak, [as in the saying]: "Are you provided for and given victory only through your weak ones?" and [the saying]: "Allah has mercy only upon those of His servants who are merciful," and spending was the character of the believers, He said, explaining that they had completely stripped themselves of humanity, so that they fear no punishment that could possibly befall them and hope for no reward that could possibly descend upon them: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾, that is, by whatever speaker it may be, ﴿"Spend"﴾, that is, upon those who have nothing, in gratitude to God for what He has delivered you from and benefited you with, through the benefit of His creatures who are His dependants. He made clear that they withhold [their wealth] from that in which they have no craft and which their hands did not produce, but from a part of it. So He said: ﴿from what God has provided you﴾. He made the provider explicit and did not use a pronoun, to indicate the greatness of the provision by the greatness of its Giver. He increased their reproach by making that apparent noun the proper name of the Essence, because it is not fitting that a servant's giving should be according to the measure of his master. So He said: ﴿God﴾, that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection. ﴿Those who disbelieve say﴾, and He made the speaker explicit, to rebuke them by the description that moves them to stinginess. So He said: ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, that is, those who concealed and covered over what the lights of their intellects had pointed them to of goodness, ﴿to those who believe﴾, that is, those who said this, who hold it as a belief, whether they were the ones who spoke to them or others who rejected it against them, mocking them, deviating from what the question demanded regarding mention of spending, toward what conveys reproach for poverty and need for food: ﴿Shall we feed﴾. They departed from the past tense so that it would not be said to them: He, glorified is He, has taken on feeding him from the time of his creation until now. So they said: ﴿him whom, if God willed, He would feed﴾, and they set a limit to Him and to His acts, so they said: [p. 138] ﴿God﴾, that is, the One who possesses all greatness, as you claim, at every time He wills it, ﴿would have fed him﴾. That is, "but we see that He does not will that, for He has not fed them, because of the poverty we see in them. So we too do not will that, in agreement with God's purpose in it." Thus they abandoned proper conduct toward the One who commands, and displayed proper conduct toward part of the will, from which they were forbidden to follow and submit to. And this did not suffice them, until they said, to the one who guided them to good, by way of conclusion from what preceded: ﴿You are only in error﴾, that is, "in what is" [i.e., "are you not, only in error"], ﴿manifest﴾, that is, encompassing you, ﴿clear﴾, that is, in the utmost clarity. They did not realize that the error is in fact theirs, because He, glorified is He, only made the feeding of some of His creatures without intermediary and of others through an intermediary as a trial from Him, to test the obedient and the disobedient, the thankful and the ungrateful, the impatient and the patient, and other of His wisdoms.

When he mentioned the scarcity of their good, which was rooted in their mockery of the Day they were reminded of, through the command to be mindful of God and the justification by hope for mercy, he followed it with the narration of another mockery from them, indicating their great ignorance in denying what they were promised. This was by way of explicitly mentioning that Day and depicting it in a manner that no one with even a little sense could fail to submit to. So he said: ﴿And they say﴾, meaning a continuous habit, added to what preceded and which entails their denial. They increased in their rebuke by using the particle of proximity (hadha, "this"), indicating that you have exceeded us [p. 139] in threatening with it and bringing it near, until one would think it was coming to us in the morning or the evening, while we have not perceived from it an eye or a trace: ﴿When is this?﴾. They increased in mockery by calling it a promise, so they said: ﴿The promise﴾, meaning that with which you threaten us, sometimes by allusion and sometimes explicitly, hasten it for us. They urged and stirred it on, increasing in denial, by their saying: ﴿If you are truthful﴾.

Since the prudent person is one who mocks nothing unless he has prepared for it with what surely averts it, [al-Biqa'i] explained their foolishness in their being struck suddenly, and that it must inevitably occur, and that it will be such as to fill the heavens and the earth, so that it is as if nothing else is in them, by His saying: ﴿ما ينظرون﴾ (they await nothing), that is, of what they are promised. It may also carry the sense of "yantazirun" (they wait for), because their delay in [believing] it takes the form of waiting, even if they intended it as mockery. He left the verb unqualified to bring it near to them, because its occurrence is certain. ﴿إلا صيحة﴾ (except a single blast). He showed the insignificance of their situation and the completeness of His power by His saying: ﴿واحدة﴾ (single). This is the first blast, the one that causes death. He confined the emphasis on oneness to this [verse], unlike what comes concerning the blast that brings them to life, because they do not deny the basic fact of death. ﴿تأخذهم﴾ (will seize them), that is, will destroy them. He showed their heedlessness by His saying: ﴿وهم يخصّمون﴾ (while they are disputing), that is, "yakhtasimun" (they dispute), that is, they quarrel over their dealings, in a state of utmost heedlessness. Perhaps He expressed it this way, indicating by the obligatory assimilation (al-idgham, merging of two identical consonants) that the doubling (al-tashdid) implies, the extreme of disputing, by establishing its causes, the highest and the lowest of them, to a limit beyond which there is no increase, because the ta' in its meaning, according to the people of God (ahl Allah, the Sufis), is the completion of causation down to its lowest level. All of this is an indication that at the time of the swoon they will be in the greatest security from it, because their turning away from it has reached a point beyond which there is no further increase. Assimilation also indicates that their disputing is in a state of utmost concealment with respect to the blast, even though the dispute reaches its utmost severity. No one read "yakhtasimun" without assimilation, indicating that no complete dispute will occur at that time such that it would be manifest. Rather, the blast destroys them before the proofs are completed and the evidences made clear. Among them are those whose companions began [the dispute], and they made it brief, by what the reading of Hamzah (one of the readers) indicates, with the khā' (خ) vowelless and the ṣād (ص) with a kasra, lightly pronounced. Among them are those whose dispute was intermediate, and in it there is concealment and elevation, by what the gemination of the ṣād (تشديد الصاد) indicates, together with ikhtilas (rapid, barely audible articulation) of the fatha on the khā' (ختلاس فتحة الخاء). Among them is one that is like this, but nearer to clarity, by what the pure fatha on the khā' (إخلاص فتحة الخاء), together with the gemination of the ṣād, indicates. Whoever read it this way with a kasra on the khā' indicated the intermediate state together with concealment and lowness. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 50:

When this was the deadly blast (al-nafkhah al-mumītah), he made the following a consequence of it: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾; that is, they will not be able to bring about a will (al-waṣiyyah) in any of (p-141) the things. The forms "al-istif'āl" and "al-taf'īl" indicate that death does not occur at the moment of hearing the first sound, but immediately after it, without any interval sufficient for the completion of some matter.

Since that does not explicitly negate walking, he said: ﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾; that is, let alone to others; ﴿they will return﴾. Rather, each one dies in his place, where the Cry (al-ṣayḥah) seizes him. Perhaps the expression with "ilā" (to) conveys that they wish to return, so they take a step, or something close to it. In a hadith: "...The Hour will certainly arrive while two men have spread their garment between them, and they will neither sell it nor fold it... The Hour will certainly arrive while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth, and he will not eat it."

When this had indicated death with certainty, he followed it with resurrection (al-ba'th); and for this reason He expressed it with the blowing (al-nafkh), for it is well known for the bestowing of the spirit (al-ruh). So He said: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾; that is, the one whose cry seized them. He left the blower unnamed (jahhalahu) as an indication that there is no dependence, in reality, on a specific blower, so that there would result from it what He - glorified is He - wills of effect. Rather, whoever God permits, whoever he may be, produces from his blowing what has been mentioned; although we know that the one permitted is Israfil - peace be upon him.

Since this blowing was the cause of their standing up before Him, equally and without any delay, He - glorified is He - expressed it with what indicates sequence (ta'aqqub), causation (tasabbub) and suddenness (fuja'a), so He said: ﴿Then, behold, they﴾; that is, at the moment of the blowing; ﴿from the graves (al-ajdath)﴾; that is, the prepared tombs, they and those in them, upon hearing that blowing; ﴿to their Lord﴾; that is, the One who was good to them by nurturing them and preparing them for this resurrection; so they denied His goodness, and not to anyone else; ﴿they will hasten (yansiluna)﴾; that is, they will quicken their walking, with short, rapid steps, with strength and vigour. How wondrous is a power that encompasses all and a wisdom that is perfect, in that a single sound gives life at one time and causes death at another; as if He had composed within it such secrets that it imparts to everything the opposite of what it is upon, of life or death, or swooning or recovery.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 52:

When the soul had become eager to hear what they would say when they beheld what they used to deny, He resumed with His saying: ﴿They will say﴾; that is: those who are among the people of woe from the general body of those who were raised by the Blast; and they are all who had died before that. Since they knew that the recompense for what they had sent ahead was every disgrace, they followed it with their saying, which Allah, glory be to Him, related as their expression at that time, because it is more painful for them: ﴿Woe to us!﴾; that is: there is nothing in our presence today that will bring us remorse except woe. (p-143) Then they asked a question, in keeping with their habit of heedlessness, and they said, making manifest what is in their hearts, specifying woe for themselves, because they are in a state of doubt: ﴿Who has raised us up from our resting place?﴾ They regarded their place in which they had been, together with what they had been in of the punishment of the barzakh, as a pleasant resting place in comparison with what was revealed to them that they would encounter of the greatest punishment. They used the singular to indicate that, despite their multitude and their dispersion, they were in the standing like a single soul. Then they recalled what they had been warned of, that Allah Himself would raise them for recompense, which is the mercy of the King toward the people of His kingdom. So they answered themselves, resuming: ﴿This is what﴾; that is: the promise which; ﴿the Most Merciful promised﴾; that is: with it. They omitted the object for generality, because they are now within the realm of affirmation. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾; that is: the one whose mercy is all-encompassing, whose mercifulness necessarily requires that there be a resurrection, so that the wronged be given justice against his wrongdoer, and that each be recompensed for his deed without injustice. He has shown mercy to us by sending the messengers to us with this; and they warned us many times of its descent, and cautioned us of its severity and its length. Since the implied sense was: "So the Most Merciful spoke truly," He joined to it His saying: ﴿And the messengers spoke truly﴾; that is: in their command; ﴿the messengers﴾; that is: those who came to us with His promise and His warning. So Allah, whose promise was given beforehand with it and who sent His messengers with it, is the One who raised us, in confirmation of His promise and of His messengers.

(p-144) Since the report of the blowing (of the Trumpet) does not negate repetition, He said—belittling the matter of resurrection in relation to His power, and showing care in emphasizing that it is a single (event)—by making the report about it an independent statement, separated from the blowing, and by using in it the verb of existence (kāna, "was"), and "in" (in), the negating particle that negates the lowest manifestations of what follows it, so how about what lies beyond it?—not "mā" (mā), which only negates completeness—: ﴿in﴾ (﴿not﴾); that is: it was not ﴿kānat﴾ (﴿was﴾); that is: the blast by which the reviving occurs; any sort of existence ﴿except a single shout﴾; that is: just as the blast of death was single; ﴿then behold they﴾; that is: suddenly, without any delay at all; ﴿all﴾; that is: in a state of being gathered together, none of them lagging behind, having no excuse for abandoning victory and continuing in submission, humiliation and abasement. And since that occurs in strange states, whose reality the intellects cannot reach, He said—turning the speech toward the manifestation of greatness, and expressing it with what is used for particular matters—﴿are brought before Us﴾ [ladaynā (before Us)]. And since that is a matter that must happen and cannot be avoided, He expressed it with the passive form, and emphasized the meaning of gathering with the plural, taking into consideration the meaning of "jamī‘" (all), and did not use the singular, out of regard for its wording, given the meaning mentioned; so He said: ﴿muḥḍarūn﴾ (﴿brought before Us﴾); that is: with the utmost reluctance on their part toward that; driven by drivers who urge them on, and by herders who subdue them.

﴿So today﴾: since this bringing forth (for judgment) is on account of justice and the manifestation of all the attributes of perfection, He said so. And since negating wrong absolutely is more eloquent than negating it from a specific person, more indicative of the intended meaning, and more concise, He said, turning the speech away from an explicit mention or a pronoun to the mode of majesty or otherwise: ﴿no soul is wronged﴾. And since the expression with that which is most often made the seat of vices, desires and deficiencies (namely "soul," nafs) is more indicative of the generality of the negation of wrong (p-145), He said: ﴿any soul﴾, that is, whatever soul it is, whether disliked or beloved. ﴿In anything﴾, that is, no wrong at all befalls it from anyone, in any matter. And since recompense in kind is more indicative of power and more inclusive of justice, He said, establishing with the address and the plural that the one whose wrong is negated is every being fit for address, lest it occur to the mind that the negated wrong concerns particular souls or a single soul: ﴿and you will not be recompensed﴾, that is, for any deed, with any portion of recompense, from anyone; ﴿except what you used to do﴾, as a settled practice of yours, by that which He set into your natures.

When he had established that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, he began to detail it, and he started with the nobler of the two groups, in answer to whoever asked about this recompense. He said, rebuking the people of wretchedness with reminder, emphasizing what they had of denial in the world, and showing eagerness for this statement and delight in it because of its great fruit: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden﴾, that is, those who have no share of the Fire. He repeated the expression "today" to magnify its importance and to emphasize its gravity, following the two blasts, the one that causes death and the one that causes standing, by mentioning some of its fruits and some of the great effects of its influence. So He said: ﴿today﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection. This indicates that their entry, or the entry of some of them, into the Garden is hastened, and that the rest remain for intercession and similar honors, while the people of the Fire enter the Fire. He expressed with what indicates that they (p-146) are wholly turned toward it, immersed in it, and directed toward it, so He said: ﴿busy with occupation﴾, that is, of a great magnitude, beyond what minds can describe, just as they were in the world in the most absorbing of occupations, striving in acts of obedience. When souls longed to know the explanation of this occupation, He said: ﴿enjoying fruits﴾, that is, they have the life of one who enjoys fruits, which is security, blessing, ease, pleasure, and complete comfort, just as they used to please us by exhausting themselves, fatiguing them, distressing them, and frightening them. The reading of Abu Ja'far (a reader of the Qur'an, i.e., a mode of recitation), with the alif omitted, is more eloquent, because it concerns the permanence of this for them, and that they themselves are in the utmost degree of lightness of spirit and goodness of conversation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 56:

Since the soul's delight is not complete except with a fitting companion, He said: ﴿They﴾; that is, with their outward forms and their inward natures; ﴿and their spouses﴾; that is, their counterparts who are in the utmost harmony with them, just as they used to leave them in their beds in the most delightful state, and line up their feet in our service while they wept; ﴿in shade﴾; that is, they will find in it the coolness of hearts and the utmost of what is desired, just as they used to roast their livers in the house of action under the heat of fasting, swallowing the bitterness of thirst, and enduring pains in pursuit of our pleasure; and they will restrain their hands and hearts from wealth by spending in charity on our paths through the passing days and the recurring nights. The reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, with a dammed ẓā' (ẓulul, ظُلُل) and the alif omitted, is for the sake of greater extension; and their agreement on the plural indicates that the shade therein varies according to the variation of deeds.

Since enjoyment is not complete except with an elevated position that enables an increase of knowledge, which causes the soul to rejoice and the eye to be delighted by the widening of sight when the gaze is extended, He said: ﴿on couches﴾; that is, elevated, adorned beds which are within canopies. Al-Baghawi said: Tha'lab said: "There is no arika (أريكة) unless there is a canopy (ḥajala) over it." Ibn Jarir said: "al-arā'ik" are canopies in which there are beds. Abu 'Ubayd related, in the Book of Virtues, from al-Hasan who said: "We did not know what al-arā'ik were until we met a man from the people of Yemen, who informed us that the arika among them is a canopy in which there is a bed." This is a recompense for their adherence to the mosques, their lowering of their gazes, and their humbling of their souls for our sake; ﴿reclining﴾; just as they used to labor in deeds, standing before us for the most part. And "al-ittikā'" is leaning to one side while relying on something that makes reliance restful, or sitting with support in the posture of one sitting cross-legged (al-mutarabbi'). The reading with a dammed kāf and the hamza omitted (muttakūn, مُتْكُون) is more indicative of sitting cross-legged and what is close to it; while the reading with a kasra on the kāf and a damma on the hamza (ittikā'an, إتْكَاءً) is more indicative of nearness to stretching out, because of the kasra in it. For it is said, as transmitted by Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qazzaz: "atkaʾtu al-rajul itkā'an" (أتْكَأْتُ الرَّجُلَ اتِّكاءً), when you prop the man up, that is, you make for him a cushion, namely a pillow on which he rests.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 57:

When he had mentioned the meanings that necessitate the eating of fruit, he brought them forth and said: ﴿For them﴾; that is, specifically for them; ﴿therein is fruit﴾; that is, fruit that never ceases at any time; so there is no impediment for them in partaking of it, and this is not restricted to mere desire. And since fruit may be applied to that which gives pleasure, he made clear that this is what is meant, and said, expressing it with the conjunction so that the fruit is mentioned twice, specifically and generally: ﴿and for them﴾. And since the context concerns the people of the Garden, who, as the Cry implies, are in it forever even though they are in this world, he left the speech without an adverbial of place, to convey the granting of their supplications in this world and the bestowal upon them of all they desire in both abodes. So he said: ﴿whatever they call for﴾; that is, whatever they seek, seeking with sincerity; either as an expression of what may occur to the soul without resolve upon it, if what is meant is things in the Garden other than the speech of God, such as foods, drinks, and the like; or as an expression of concern, if what is meant is that it is His speech, glory be to Him. This is because in the world they would wean their souls from desires, abstaining from what perishes and aspiring to what is with Us of the enduring good deeds.

Then he explained "what they ask for" (yaddaʿūna, i.e. what they seek) by the extreme of longing for it. Or he began a new statement about it with His words: ﴿Peace﴾; that is, (it is) very great, whose description cannot be fully grasped; ﴿upon you, O people of Paradise﴾; it exists, He is (it); or it is what is spoken, He is (it). And peace (salām) encompasses all blessings. Then he clarified the state of this peace by what he showed of its greatness, with His words: ﴿a word from a Lord﴾; that is, one of constant beneficence; ﴿Most Merciful﴾; that is, of great honour, by what the Divinity is pleased with, just as they used to do in the world, doing everything in which there is good pleasure; so He shows them mercy in the state of peace and hearing speech, with the delight of seeing (Him), together with strengthening them against astonishment and swooning at the magnitude of the matter, and with qualifying them for this most noble station, despite their inability to reach it. This context has made clear that it is from Allah (exalted be He) without an intermediary, for He emphasised it with "word," with the inceptive particle, and with the mention of attributes of beneficence, as Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said: "There is no doubt that nothing equals this in bliss, coolness of the eye, nobility, and loftiness of rank." And there is no doubt that this is truly the intended goal, for it is the core of bliss on that Day, which is truly the core of existence, in hiddenness, in goodness, and in corruption. Thus it is established that this verse is the core of this surah, just as this surah was the core of the Qur'an.

A hadith has been reported in the Tafsir of al-Baghawi and in Kitab al-Mi'atayn by Ustadh Abu 'Uthman al-Sabuni, that it is from Allah (exalted be He) without an intermediary, from Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them, so they raise their heads, and behold, the Lord (exalted be He) has looked down upon them from above them, and says: 'Peace be upon you, O people of Paradise.' This is His saying (exalted be He): ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. So He looks at them, and they look at Him, and they do not turn to anything of bliss as long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and blessing remain in their abodes."

Abu 'Uthman said: This is a hadith strange (gharib) in both its chain and its text; I do not know that I have written it except through this route.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 59:

Since the implied sense is: "So look, and increase in regret, O guilty ones," he follows it with His saying: ﴿And separate yourselves﴾; that is, withdraw into a separation that is entirely purposeful. He follows the established pattern of intensifying the terror of that station by repeating His saying: ﴿today﴾; that is, away from My righteous servants, or away from those among them who remain with you at the station, so that they may be purified of their defilements and healed of their harms, because the absence of the watcher is the most complete bliss, and the distance of the enemy is the highest joy. He omitted the vocative particle, not out of closeness of honor, but to indicate (p-151) that they are in the grip, with no obstacle to the utmost disposal over them in whatever is desired, since nothing stands between them and it. ﴿O guilty ones﴾; that is, those deeply immersed in criminality, so that it does not occur to your imaginations that you would mix with them at all today. This is like how you used to separate yourselves from them in the world and shun them out of haughtiness and arrogance. So this is His saying to the guilty, and that is His saying to the believers. It is therefore sound that it is a reversal (qalb), because through it the righteousness of some of the accountable is achieved and the corruption of others, which is the completion of the righteousness of the first group. This has been discussed earlier at the beginning of surah "al-Rum," and what is beneficial is to recall it here.

(p-152) When He commanded them to separate, a volitional command with judicial force, they separated at once. They concealed their regret, remorse fell upon their hands, they bit their fingertips and gnashed their teeth, their eyes stared fixedly, their faces darkened, their lips shrank, their heads hung down, their colours faded, and they were dragged upon their faces. There was, among the kinds of distress and the circumstances of anguish, what the intellects cannot grasp, what the souls melt at the mention of, and what makes the hearts tear loose. He, glorified is He, addressed them in that state, rebuking them with this speech and giving the reason for His judgment against them: that He did not leave them neglected. Rather, He fashioned in them intellects and set up for them, as proofs of His perfection, what is sufficient for their salvation. Then He did not leave them to that alone, but sent them messengers and sent down to them scriptures. ﴿Did I not charge you﴾, that is: I enjoined upon you a great charge, through the proofs I had set up, the intellects I had bestowed, the messengers I had sent, and the books I had sent down, in clarifying the path that leads to salvation. He turned the speech away from the manifestation of beneficence to what is more fitting for it than the manifestation of speaking in the first person singular, to remove ambiguity. Then He indicated His exaltedness, majesty, greatness and the sublimity of His perfection, so He said: ﴿to you﴾.

Since the purpose of this address is to reproach them, rebuke them and confound them, and since this surah is the heart, and the heart is the noblest of the organs, and man is the noblest of existent things, He singled them out with the address, because His address is also an address to the jinn. So He said, emphasizing what the particle of limit (ḥarf al-ghāyah, "to the end") conveyed of the height of his rank and the greatness of his station, through what the particle of distance indicated: ﴿O children of Adam﴾, that is: I did not single you out with this over the children of other than your kind, so that this specification would become a cause for you to disobey, but rather so that it would necessitate acts of obedience and knowing. ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾, that is: the distant one, the one burned by your obedience to him in what he whispers to you. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition against worshipping him with what requires intense aversion from him, after having hinted at that by describing him. So He said: ﴿Indeed, he is to you﴾, with emphasis because their conduct was the conduct of one who believes in his friendship, ﴿an enemy manifest﴾, that is: openly hostile in the extreme. This is from the standpoint of his enmity toward your father, the enmity that expelled you from the Garden, than which there is no more noble abode; and from the standpoint of his commanding you what makes this world hateful, such as disagreement and quarrelling; and from the standpoint of his adorning for you the perishable, which no intelligent person would desire even if it had no defect except its perishing. How much more so when most of it is turbidity, filth and pollution! How much more so when it preoccupies one from the enduring! How much more so when it becomes an obstacle from the Master! How much more so when it angers Him and veils one from Him!

Since He had rebuked them by reminding them of what they had committed, together with the prohibition against worshipping the enemy (giving priority to averting corruptions), He rebuked them by reminding them of what they had neglected, together with the taking of covenants, as an obligation of commanding the worship of the Protector. So He said, conjoining it to "allā" (that you should not): ﴿And that you should worship Me﴾. And when He, glory be to Him, reminded them of the command to worship Him, He made known its excellence, urging them to adhere to it before that Day, saying: ﴿This is a straight path﴾; that is, the command to worship Me; ﴿a straight path﴾; that is, one that is eloquent in its guidance (balīgh al-qawm). Whereas the worship of Satan is a narrow, crooked path, in the utmost degree of narrowness and crookedness.

When the intended sense was: "You followed him and took his path, despite its crookedness, and you abandoned my path, despite the evident uprightness of it," He connected to it His saying: ﴿And he had certainly led astray from among you﴾, meaning away from the clear, straight way, by the whispering I had empowered him with. He emphasized it (p-154) to indicate that it is a matter that is hardly believable, because its commission is far-fetched in the ordinary course, given the clarity of its affair and the manifestness of its corruption and harm. Since the human being is of stubborn disposition and high resolve when he wills something, He expressed it with His saying: ﴿jibillan﴾, meaning great, mighty nations, who were like mountains in the strength of their resolutions and the difficulty of their submission. Yet he played with them as he pleased. Glory be to Him who empowered him to do so; otherwise, he is weaker in plotting and more contemptible in affair.

In the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit of al-Fayruzabadi), he said: "al-Jubl" (الجُبْل), with a damma, is dry trees, and a group of people, like "al-Jubul" (الجُبُل), like "unuq" (عُنُق), "adl" (عِدْل), "utul" (عُتُلّ), "timirr" (طِمِرّ), "timirrah" (طِمِرَّة), and "amir" (أمِير). Then he said: and with a kasra and with a damma, and like "timirrah" (طِمِرَّة), it means a nation and a group. Then he said: "al-Jubla" (الجُبْلَة), with three vowelings and with a vowel-transposed form, and like "timirrah," means creation and nature.

The reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir (qira'at, the recognized Qur'anic readings), with a damma on the jim, a sukun on the ba', and a light lam, indicates those who are at the first level of intensity and strength. The reading of Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ruways from Ya'qub, with two dammas and lightening, indicates what is above that, which approaches the middle, together with prominence and height, because of the damma, from strength. The reading of Rawh is similar, with a shadda (p-155), indicating what is above the middle. These readings are indicated by the vowel markings, and the shadda; but it is with obscurity, and as if it were with cunning, as indicated by the fact that both vowels are with a kasra.

Glory be to Him, He magnified the matter with His saying: ﴿a great deal﴾. Then He increased the rebuke and denunciation with what the situation produces and what his misleading them caused, together with the intellects they were given, from His saying: ﴿Then will you not reason?﴾ Since He, glory be to Him, had given them intellects, and what intellects!, He expressed it with the verb "to be," saying: ﴿that you may be reasoning﴾, meaning, so that your intellects would guide you to what contains salvation, through the proofs I have set up, and what the messengers alerted to and warned against, such as the destruction of those before you because of following the devils, and other than that, of every clear and manifest matter.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 63:

When He rebuked them for doing the deed of one who has no intellect, He said, completing the disgrace: ﴿This is Hell﴾; "This" is a pointing to something present, either the state of standing at its brink or being pushed into it; ﴿Hell﴾ — that is, the one that will meet you with scowling and frowning, just as you used to treat My righteous servants; ﴿which you were﴾ — that is, a state into which I prepared you for accepting what can be possible, by the intellects I planted in you; and since what was to be feared was the threat of it, not its occurrence from a specific person, He said — using the passive form — ﴿you are promised﴾; that is, if you do not turn back from your error.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 64:

﴿Burn in it today﴾; that is: taste its heat, its blaze, and its roaring; and (to emphasize) the terror of the matter of that day, by repeating mention of it in the manner already passed. So He said: ﴿today﴾, so that you may be occupied with a preoccupation, as the companions of the Garden were occupied; and how far apart are the two preoccupations. ﴿Because of what﴾; that is: because of the cause of what.

And since they had steeled themselves in transgression, with the steeling of one who is disposed to it, He explained this by mentioning the state of being: so He said: ﴿you used to disbelieve﴾; that is: you used to cover up what is very manifest to your intellects from My signs, renewing that repeatedly and persisting in it.

When it was as though it were said: "Will He judge them by His knowledge, or will He carry out the matter according to the rule of this world, which is acting on evidence?", He made clear that it is according to a more apparent rule than the rules of this world. So He said, magnifying the Day, following the preceding pattern of manifesting greatness, since that is more fitting for awe: ﴿Today We shall seal upon their mouths﴾. That is, by what We possess of wondrous power, branching out from greatness. He turned the speech to the third person, signalling turning away and because of the intensity of anger, and said: ﴿upon their mouths﴾. That is, because of their audacity in lying in the Hereafter, as was their habit in this world. Deceit, lying and corruption occur only through the tongue, which expresses what is in the heart. As for the rest of the limbs, however much God breaks custom by enabling them to speak, they speak only the truth. Therefore He said: ﴿and their hands will speak to Us﴾. That is, concerning what they did, as an acknowledgement which is the greatest testimony. ﴿And their feet will bear witness﴾ (p-157) that is, against them, with a clear speech, which, along with being a testimony of acknowledgement, ﴿for what they used to earn﴾. That is, in this world, by their natures.

The verse employs ihtibak (a device in which something is omitted from each of two parallel parts, the omitted element in one being indicated by the mention in the other): it first attributes speech to the hands, because they were the ones directly engaged, as an indication that it is omitted from the part concerning the feet; and it secondly attributes testimony to the feet, because they were present, as an indication that it is omitted from the part concerning the hands. The evidence for this is that the statement of the one directly engaged is an acknowledgement, while the statement of the one present is a testimony.

Muslim related in his Sahih, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The servant will say: 'O Lord, did You not protect me from injustice?' He said: 'He will say: "Yes."' Then he will say: 'Indeed, I do not permit against myself except a witness from myself.' He will say: '(Your own soul suffices against you today as a witness, and the noble recording angels as witnesses.)' Then his mouth will be sealed, and his limbs will be told: 'Speak!' So they will speak of his deeds. Then he will be left free between himself and speech, and he will say: 'Away with you! Destruction! It was for your sake that I was contending.'"

The apparent wisdom in sealing his mouth is to prevent him from babbling and shouting during their testimony against him, so that their speech is not heard, as is the habit of those given to obstinacy during disputes.

Al-Biqa'i, *Nazm al-Durar*, on Surah 36, verse 66:

When he had completed the presentation of the parable and what follows it, the indication of the meaning of: ﴿You can only warn the one who follows the Reminder﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:11), and of what it was used to establish concerning the bringing back to life of the dead, and when he had shown this by what he left, such as the sun, which is free of ambiguity, and had added from the seas of benefits and beautiful lessons what fills the universe of the requirements of faith, and had mentioned what awaits the two groups, those who follow and those who refuse, on the Day of Resurrection, and had concluded with the sealing of the mouths after the Resurrection, he followed it with the verse about the sealing by obliteration and transformation before death, as a threat, joining it to what the meaning had returned to from what was said at the beginning of that address, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles upon their necks﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:8), and so on. This was to repel what might occur to someone's mind, that power does not extend to anything other than obliterating the meanings, by striking the barrier and what is similar to it. So He informed that, just as He blinded their insights, He is able to take away their sight. He said, emphasizing what they hold of denial, or of the acts that are the deeds of one who denies: ﴿And if﴾. He expressed it with the present tense in His saying: ﴿We will﴾, so that it would be anticipated at every moment, and this would be more forceful in threat. ﴿We would have obliterated﴾, and He restricted the verb, indicating that the meaning is: if We willed, We would have brought about the obliteration which We placed upon their insights, ﴿upon their eyes﴾, so We would have removed their eye and its trace, and made it level with the face, such that it would become as though it had never existed at all. The explanation of this meaning has already been reported from Ibn Hisham in the chapter on "al-Nisa'".

When the one sitting with a person in a gathering of dispute, while he is threatening him that if he does not turn back from his error, he will strike him with a calamity, is struck by a great misfortune, he hastens to flee, out of fear of something else, following his nature, because of the bewilderment that has seized him and the great alarm and dread that has touched him. This is what befell the people of Lut, peace be upon him, when Jibril, peace be upon him, wiped over their eyes and covered them, when they rushed toward the door fleeing, saying: "Lut has the most sorcerous of people." He linked to that His saying: ﴿So they raced﴾, meaning: they imposed that upon themselves and brought it about. Since the intended purpose was to show their haste in fleeing, he made the verb transitive by implying in it the meaning of "they rushed", as He said (Most High): ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:148), and so He said: ﴿the path﴾, meaning the clear road which they were accustomed to, which they knew and frequented, and of which they had the utmost knowledge. Since the blind person cannot, in such a situation, walk without a guide, let alone race, he linked to that His saying, in denial: ﴿How﴾, meaning: in what manner, and from where, ﴿could they see﴾? Meaning: they did not find the path, because they could not see, but rather they collided with one another and fell into ruin, and were destroyed.

When all of this was accompanied by the capacity for movement, He said: ﴿And if We willed﴾, that is, that We would transform them (*maskh*), ﴿We would have transformed them﴾, that is, We would have turned them into inanimate matter (*jamadiyya*), thereby nullifying in them voluntary movement. Since the purpose was the suddenness of these calamities, as a demonstration that He, glorified is He, faces no difficulty in any of that, He said: ﴿in their places﴾, that is, the place that was theirs before the transformation, each one of them occupying it by sitting, standing, or otherwise, in that specific spot only, before moving from it. This is the meaning of Shu'ba's *qira'a* (a canonical recitation transmitted from 'Asim): "*makanatihim*" (in their places, plural). It indicates that the intended meaning is the transformation into states of inanimate matter, as is implied by what follows from it in His saying: ﴿then they would not be able﴾, that is, by their own means, ﴿to proceed﴾ (*mudiyyan*) with any kind of effort, that is, movement in any direction. Then He joined to the conditional clause His saying: ﴿nor would they return﴾, that is, a return to their former state, before the transformation, would occur for them in some manner. This indicates that these matters are true, and not as they claim, that they are imagination and sorcery. Rather, their permanence is such that no one among creation can lift it or change it by any kind of alteration of this sort, if God wills. Had it been said "*wa la rujū'an*" (nor a return), as some have said is the intended meaning, this precious sense would not have been conveyed.

When these were matters of obligation, some stubborn and contentious opponents could dispute them out of arrogance. Since his being the Prophet of mercy (ﷺ) prevented a sudden punishment by the torment of annihilation, He pointed to them through what they witness of His manifest power and wondrous wisdom in His creation. So He said, using the conjunction (fa) to indicate an unstated thing to which it is joined, on the premise that the sense is: "We created them as drops of semen (nutfan), then as clots of blood ('alaqan), then as lumps of flesh (mudghan), then We brought them forth as infants who know nothing and are capable of nothing. Then We advanced them through the stages of their years, raising them up through the levels of outward and inward powers, until they reached the limit of maturity (al-ashudd), which is the completion of human powers. Then We halted their outward and inward powers, and did not, according to the customary order, bring about in them at that time a power that they did not have in the days of youth (p-161)." So: ﴿And whoever We give long life﴾, that is, We prolong his life greatly after that; ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾. The reading of 'Asim and Hamza, with a damma on the first letter, a fatha on the second, and a kasra on the kaf with shadda, indicates that people differ in the degree of their reversal. He did not say "in His creation" (fi khalqihi), lest it be thought that the one given long life has a creation which He originated and devised. ﴿In the creation﴾ means: in what We devised of the formation of his body and his spirit. That is, We return him to his former state, descending along the same stages by which We raised him, until his sensory powers wane, so that he becomes like a child, unable to do anything, and his mental powers wane, so that he knows nothing. Whoever is able to effect such a transformation from one state to another that did not exist before, by direct and reverse order, is able to effect the same kind of transformation as what has passed, without any difference. However, because of their great familiarity with this, they regard it as easy, and because the first kind of existence is rare among them, they regard it as remote. For this reason He made His words a consequence of what preceded, using the style of the past in the recitation of the majority, and turning to address (the audience) in the reading of the Medinans and Ya'qub, since that is closer to moving the heart, and to inform that exhortation is general for everyone fit to be addressed: ﴿Will they not then understand?﴾ Some of the knowers (al-'arifin) said: He restricted the matter to creation to exclude command (al-amr), for the one who is commanded grows in obedience to his Lord and in knowledge of Him as he grows in years. That is, the reversal in the body is something unavoidable, whereas in matters of knowledge it is sometimes so and sometimes not.

[p. 162] When He, glory be to Him, had completed the proof, in the verse ﴿Certainly the word has come true against most of them﴾ (Yasin 36:7), that denial applies to the two foundations, tawhid (the oneness of God) and hashr (the gathering for resurrection), and had made both clear in the fullest clarification, He turned to establishing the third foundation, which is the command of the Messenger and the revelation (tanzil). Since it is well known that Allah has established the custom among human beings that whoever reaches the age of forty-two, having passed the years of childhood and youth, his natural dispositions become fixed, so that no new disposition is added to him, and all his powers come to a halt, so that nothing more is added to them. As for sensory faculties, this holds absolutely. As for intellectual faculties, they increase only through experience and acquisition. For this reason they said:

*When a man in his youth finds manliness beyond his reach,*
*Seeking it in his maturity will be very hard for him.*

It is also well known that the prophets, peace be upon them, display natural gifts of knowledge, wisdom and other things which Allah brings about through their hands, and none of their powers decreases; rather they are increased. This is as has been related: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to walk without any hurry, while the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, would exert themselves so much that their greatest effort was to keep up with his pace of unhurried walking. And he wrestled with Rukanah, who was a byword for strength, and Rukanah was confident in himself that he would throw whoever wrestled with him. Yet the Prophet (ﷺ) overcame him, and he returned to this three times; each time, Rukanah could not hold firm in his grip, until he began to say: "This is astonishing, O Muhammad! Will you throw me down?" And he went round to his wives, who were nine, each one of them nine times in a single night. [p. 163] And there are other accounts of his powers, by which he surpassed people. No prophet, among those who lived a thousand years or less, is reported to have lost any of his powers. Indeed, it is recorded in the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "The Angel of Death, peace be upon him, was sent to Musa, peace be upon him, to take his soul. When he came to him, Musa struck him and gouged out his eye. So the angel returned to his Lord and said: 'You sent me to a servant who does not want death.' He said: 'Return to him and tell him to place his hand upon the back of a bull, and for every hair his hand covers he will have a year.' He said: 'O Lord, then what?' He said: 'Death.' He said: 'Then now.'"

And at the end of the Torah: "So Abd Allah Musa died there in the land of Moab, at the command of the LORD. And he was buried in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows his grave to this day. Moses was a hundred and twenty years old when he died; his eye was not dim, nor was his vigour abated."

Since the matter is as described, and since Allah, glory be to Him, made the sending of the prophets occur in the years when natural dispositions stand still and powers weaken, as a breach of the normal custom, to honour them and to alert people to their truthfulness, it is understood from the conjunction (of the verse) with no preceding element to which it is conjoined, and from the use of a pronoun referring to him (ﷺ) without any prior mention of him, that the implied meaning is: "But our Prophet (ﷺ), We let him live long, and We did not reverse him, but We granted him natural dispositions of excellence, which the first and the last were unable to attain. So he brought a Qur'an which rendered jinn and humankind powerless, and knowledge and blessings that surpassed all powers." It is certain that what he brought is not poetry, contrary to what they accused him of, out of rebellion, enmity, and lying against him, and fabrication and exaggeration in slander and tyranny. For the years of childhood and youth had passed over him entirely, and he never composed a verse of poetry, even though you and people like you find in it pride and boasting. And he reached the age of settled maturity, in which it is certain that no new natural disposition arises in a person that was not present in his youth, whether poetic or otherwise. So ﴿We did not teach him poetry﴾, that is, We did not teach him, ﴿poetry﴾, in what We taught him, which is to force oneself to be bound by a known metre, an intended rhyme, and a rhyme-sound that one commits to, and to turn meanings around it, and to drag words to it by force, as Zuhayr did in his annual odes (hawliyyat), and as others among the artificers did. ﴿Nor is it fitting for him﴾ (Yasin 36:69). ﴿I am not of the pretenders﴾ (Sad 38:86). For that, although you consider it a source of pride, is not befitting to Our dignity, because only one who wishes to promote and adorn his speech by shaping it upon a known and intended metre and a committed rhyme takes pleasure in it, since he cannot produce something better without that, something incomparable without commitment to metre or rhyme. Moreover, there is another defect in it, which is the greatest cause of aversion: it must necessarily weaken some of the meanings through the commitment to it. [p. 165] Since We did not teach him this baseness, We formed him upon all the arts of eloquence, and empowered him over every aspect of fluency. Then We placed within his heart the springs of wisdom, and trained him to express lofty meanings, even subtle ones, in strong, sweet, easy words, whether metrical or not. This was by what We inspired in him, and then by what Gabriel, peace be upon him, conveyed to him, of the comprehensive words and speech which We commanded him to deliver. So there is no artificiality in him at all. Whenever he was given the choice between two matters, he chose the easier of them, so long as it was not sinful or a severing of kinship ties.

This line I have quoted is attributed in al-Hamasa, at the beginning of the chapter on adab, to a man of the Banu Qurayʿ, whose name it does not mention, and before it are:

*Whenever people see the wealthy man and his neighbour is poor, they say: he is incompetent, or he is hardy.*

*Wealth and poverty are not from a person's own effort, but rather fortunes are distributed and fates decreed.*

*When a man in his youth finds manliness beyond his reach, seeking it in his maturity will be very hard for him.*

*How many a wealthy man we have seen who is blamed, and a poor vagrant of a people who dies while being praised.*

The meaning is that abundance and scarcity of wealth are not from any natural disposition; rather, it is a divine matter, in which natural dispositions, whether of vigour or otherwise, have no role. The evidence is that we often see one who lacked wealth in his youth, when he was vigorous, and then attained it in old age when he was weak; and we have seen one who failed to attain manliness in youth attain it in old age. And the evidence is that many a wealthy man has blameworthy natural dispositions, and many a poor man has praiseworthy character. Manliness is humanity, and it is every matter that is agreeable and praiseworthy in its outcome, good in its end; and this is nobility. The meaning is that whoever has manliness in his natural disposition, his nature drives him to practise it in his youth, whether he is rich or poor; and whoever does not have it cannot force himself to attain it in the years of maturity. How excellent they were, how wise, how perceptive of subtleties, and how knowledgeable! That is why this unlettered Prophet was made one of them, so that his knowledge filled the universe and rose through the ranks of meanings, and in comparison with it, Kiwan (Saturn) is nothing!

Since poetry, together with the artificiality upon which it is built, which is very far from the character of the prophets, how much more so from the most noble of them, is something acquired through it in praise and satire, and most of it is therefore falsehood, along with other defects, He, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿Nor is it fitting for him﴾, that is, it is neither proper, nor sought after, nor possible at all, because his station is too exalted, and his aspiration too high, to be a eulogist or a satirist, or to bind himself to what may lead to a defect in meaning; his nature is utterly incompatible with that. [p. 167] Since the proof concerning the command of the Messenger (ﷺ) has been completed, and it has been established that poetry, which is the deliberate shaping of speech upon a known metre and a committed rhyme, is a defect for the reasons mentioned, and because commitment to metre, to the rhyming sound, and to the rhyme necessarily entails advancing and delaying, and hinting at meanings without clear expression or explanation, so that it becomes hard to understand and difficult to express; and He negated that defect from him (ﷺ), this implies the purification of what was revealed to him from it, as the plural of majesty in "We taught" indicates. He established for him what befits him. So He said, as a justification of what came before: ﴿It is not﴾, that is, this which he has brought you, ﴿except a reminder﴾, that is, an honour and an admonition; ﴿and a Qur'an﴾, that is, one that encompasses all wisdom, both worldly and otherworldly, recited in the sanctuaries, repeated in acts of worship, and through its recitation and its practice one attains the success of both abodes, together with the distinction between what is confusing; ﴿clear﴾, that is, manifest in this, making plain all that is in it to whoever seeks it as he should, and who seeks it at its highest price, after sharing in its general understanding and its mere pleasure: the intelligent and the dull, the sharp and the slow. It is not artificial poetry, in which, by the necessity of commitment to metre, rhyme and rhyming sound, something is brought forward from its exact place at one time, delayed at another, or replaced by something that does not equal it, so that its meanings are diminished and become complicated and obscure, so that none understands it except this one and that one, [p. 168] and even so, it is one of the whisperings of the devils. How far apart are the two! This meaning is made utterly clear at the end of Sad: ﴿Say: I ask of you no reward for it, nor am I of the pretenders﴾ (Sad 38:86), ﴿It is only a reminder for the worlds﴾ (Sad 38:87), that is, for all of them, the intelligent and the dull alike; unlike poetry, which, although it falls very far short of eloquence, is a reminder only for the very intelligent.

[p. 169] When He mentioned the Messenger's (ﷺ) matter in what He gave him of the marks of nobility, in the setting of the reversal for others, He mentioned the reason for that, saying: ﴿That he may warn﴾. That is, the Messenger (ﷺ) is the one who warns. The evidence for this is what the context indicates by the implied meaning, and the shift to second-person address in the reading of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub supports it, indicating that no one understands it in its true sense except him (ﷺ).

Since this Qur'an is clear, and the Messenger (ﷺ) is characterized by it, he is its manifestation and the image of its surah. His condition therefore required that no living person remain behind in faith. He said, making explicit what in the first view should have been a pronoun, to convey generality, and clarifying that His judgment, glory be to Him, prevented that: the warned were divided into two groups. ﴿Whoever is﴾, as a firmly established state, ﴿alive﴾, that is, in complete spiritual life, which becomes a cause of everlasting life. Such a person does not hesitate in faith in him, out of fear of what he warns of, matters about which no doubt at all can be entertained. So good is hoped for him, and he is a believer in reality, even if at the beginning of his affair the opposite appeared in him.
