He used the singular pronoun here according to the wording, indicating the scarcity of the fortunate, and used the plural in the second case according to the meaning, to inform of the abundance of the wretched. ﴿And the word may be justified﴾, that is, be due and be established, ﴿the word﴾, that is, the punishment, ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, that is, those deeply immersed in disbelief, for they are dead in reality even if you see them as living. So the verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device of mutual omission, in which each half implies what is omitted from the other): faith is omitted in the first part because its opposite is mentioned in the second, and death is omitted in the second part because its opposite is mentioned in the first. From this it is established that the greatest incompatibility between the Qur'an and poetry, and likewise rhymed prose (saj'), is that it is entirely serious. Its methods aim primarily at meanings, and the wording follows. The poet and the rhymer, by contrast, primarily aim at the rhyme letter (al-rawwi), the rhyme, and the closing rhyme-unit (al-fasila). This may even lead to weakness of meaning and of speech, departing from reality. This is inevitable, as Hassan ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him) said, and his condition is well known for eloquence, variety in speech methods, sincerity of tone, and excellence in Islam, in the expedition of al-Ghaba. Its commander was Sa'd ibn Zayd al-Ashhali (may Allah be pleased with him):

"Tell the sons of the lowborn woman that we are at peace on the morning of the horsemen of al-Miqdad."

Sa'd became angry with Hassan (may Allah be pleased with both of them), and swore that he would never speak to him again, and said: "Go to my horses and my horsemen, and give them to al-Miqdad." Hassan apologized to him and praised him with verses, and said: "By Allah, I did not intend that. But the rhyme letter coincided with the name al-Miqdad, because the poem is in the letter dal." The Prophet (ﷺ) never had the intention of wording in his mind, for that belongs to the category of tarwiq (ornamenting verse for its own sake). He (ﷺ) was entirely serious, so he did not deviate from a thing because it was metrical, but because it would not convey the meaning. Just as the Arabs avoid solecism and do not speak it well, nor do their tongues accustom themselves to it, because it is a solecism, not because it is a movement. If something of the metrical coincides with the intended meaning for the purpose of conveying the meaning, he says it, as happens to many authors: metrical speech that they intended. And as much metrical speech from all the meters of poetry occurs in the Qur'an. If it did not coincide with the meaning, he would not have said it. On this basis is to be understood his saying (ﷺ):

"I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of Abd al-Muttalib,"

which, if the humans and the jinn united to bring forth what he conveyed of meaning in his words, or their equivalents in a different arrangement, they would not be able to do it. When you consider every line he quoted and altered, you will not find that he altered it except for a sublime meaning that cannot be achieved within the meter, or else there is no difference between his delivery of it metrically and in altered form. The same is true of saj'. From this it is known that the meaning is not that the meter is inherently bad, but that deliberately aiming at meter and rhymed prose is a deficiency unbefitting his lofty station, because the poet is restricted by a meter, a rhyme letter and a rhyme. If the meaning obeys him together with what he is restricted by, well and good; otherwise he resorts to tricks to complete what he is restricted by, even if the meaning suffers. The rhymer is close to this. This is what Allah did not teach him, because he (ﷺ) follows meanings, realities and wisdoms that yield everlasting life, being disposed by his upright nature to that and not disposed to anything else through artifice. If you reflect deeply on the end of the verse, which is a justification of what precedes it, you will realize that this is what is meant. It becomes most clear from this that each of the two is a deficiency, so none of his noble character moves toward them, and he has no concern for them at all. I have fully elaborated on this and perfected it in my book Masa'id al-Nazar li'l-Ishraf 'ala Maqasid al-Suwar (Ascents of Reflection for Overseeing the Aims of the Surahs), which serves as an introduction to this book. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is right.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 71:

When He—glory be to Him—had informed them of the blinding of their thoughts, threatened them with the obliteration of their eyes and the transforming of them (into stone) upon their seats and their resting places, and made known that His Book is a seal upon their warning, He reminded them of His power, and confirmed this, by way of establishing it, through the wonders of His craftsmanship. So He said, conjoining it to what its implied sense requires: "Have they not seen what We have brought forward and what the verse 'and whomever We cause to live long' has made understood, and what follows of the wonders of Our making, by allusion and by explicit statement, which indicate Our all-encompassing knowledge and Our complete power? Whenever We direct Our speech toward it, the word becomes binding upon it, no obstacle prevents it, and no repeller of it can be imagined." — ﴿Have they not seen﴾; that is: that they should know with a knowledge that is like sight, which is more evident to them as an indication in their most noble possessions. And it is not far from my view—though the distance be long—that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [Yasin: 31]. The former is a solicitation toward His Oneness through warning of vengeances, and this is through reminding of blessings. And He drew their attention to the greatness in that by presenting the speech in its manifestation, as He did in the verse about the destruction of the generations. So He said: ﴿that We created for them﴾, and He specified it by His own noble Self, erasing intermediate causes and showing their honour through the honouring of it, in His saying: ﴿from what Our hands have made﴾. And since man is bound by the faculty of imagination, from which he never separates, and for this reason he sees spirits in dreams in the forms of our bodies, and since the hand was the locus of His power and the place of His specific attention, He expressed to him by what he understands, and so He said: ﴿Our hands﴾; that is, without intermediary, with knowledge from Us of their powers, their measures, their benefits, their natures, and other matters of their affairs; ﴿cattle﴾. Then He clarified that they belong to them by what follows from their creation, in His saying: ﴿so they are their owners﴾; that is, controllers, subduers, without any power of their own over that, were it not for Our power by way of causation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 72:

(p-173) Since ownership does not necessarily entail submission, He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿And We have made them subservient to them﴾; that is, We made their leading easy. Had We willed, We would have made them wild, as We made what is smaller than them and weaker. So whoever is able to subdue very difficult things for others is able to make things submit to himself. Then He gave as the consequence of this His saying: ﴿Of them is their riding﴾; that is, that which they ride, and it is the camels, because they are the greatest of their mounts, given the all-encompassing benefit of them in that respect and their abundance. And for the sake of such a reminder of the great blessing and benefit, and of the independence of each of the two blessings in itself, he repeated the preposition (min) and used the present tense to indicate renewal, by the renewal of slaughtering, unlike the mount, whose suitability for that is constant and enduring. So He said: ﴿and of them they eat﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 73:

When he indicated the great benefit of riding and eating, by placing the prepositional phrase first, and its benefits apart from that were numerous, he said: ﴿And for them therein are benefits﴾; that is, from their wool, their fur, their hair, their hides, their sale, and other things. He specified drink from the general category of benefits, because of its wide-ranging benefit, and so he said, gathering it (all) together, given the differing tastes of the milk of the three kinds (of livestock)—and it is as if he expressed it with the final term of the plurals, because of the differing tastes of the individual members of a single kind, for one who reflects—: ﴿and drinks﴾; that is, of the milk, which We brought forth distinct from the excrement and the blood, pure and delicious. All of this has no cause except that Our word has been realized concerning it, so it could not but be in accordance with what We willed. So let him who is weaker in condition than them beware of the rights of Our command and the execution of Our judgment in what displeases him.

When these things were of such great magnitude that, were a person to lack them, his livelihood would be disturbed, he thereby caused the resumption of the rebuke against them for their failure to obey Him, by his saying: ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾; that is, will they bring about gratitude, which is the glorification of the Benefactor for what He has bestowed; and this is an interrogative with the meaning of a command.

When He had reminded them of His blessings and warned them of His retribution, He expressed wonder at their low outlook and the ugliness of their effects. So He said, rebuking them, reproaching them, silencing them, and marvelling at the increase in their misguidance, shifting from the manifestation of Greatness to something greater than it: ﴿And they have taken﴾. That is, We did that for them, while the situation was that they had imposed on themselves something other than what the primordial nature (al-fitrah, the innate disposition) guides them to, in that they took. Or it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "kanu" (they were) in His saying: ﴿except that they used to mock at him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30]. In that case the sense is: "except that they used to renew their mockery; and they took, before His sending a messenger to them, along with what they saw of Our power and what they received of Our blessing, in it." ﴿Besides Allah﴾: that is, the One who possesses all greatness, so everything is beneath Him, and whatever is beneath Him is subdued and owned. ﴿Gods﴾: that is, having no share of power nor any fitness for divinity. Since it was established that they are not fit for what they have qualified them for, the listener became eager to ask about (p-175) the cause of that. So He said, as an answer to that and a marvelling at their condition: ﴿Perhaps they﴾: that is, the worshippers. Since their aim was to obtain help from whatever helper there might be, He used the passive form (bana li-l-maf'ul) in His saying ﴿they may be helped﴾ (yunsarun): that is, so that their state, in their own assumption, while gathered around them and bound to them, would be like the state of one who is aided against one who opposes him, contends with him, and sets himself against him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 75:

When victory has two causes, one outward, which is gathering together (al-ijtima'), and one inward and original, which is the god upon whom the gathering is made, he (Allah) made clear their error by the squandering of hope. So he said, as a resumptive statement (mustaani'an) in answer to one who seems to have asked: "Did they then attain what they wanted?": ﴿They are not able﴾; that is, the gods that were taken; ﴿to help them﴾; that is, the worshippers; ﴿and they﴾; that is, the worshippers; ﴿for them﴾; that is, for the gods; ﴿are an army﴾. Since the word "jund" is shared between an army (al-'askar), helpers (al-a'wan), and a city (al-madinah), he specified the intended meaning by the plural pronoun, and because it is more indicative of their incapacity and worthlessness, he said: ﴿brought forth (muhdarun)﴾; that is, they act in gathering to them and in defending them, like one who is gathered unwillingly by the rule of a kingdom and the governance of greatness. Thus the lesson concerns them alone in obtaining the outward cause, together with their worship of the powerless and their humiliation before the weak and lowly, along with what they claim of nobility, pride, and grandeur. Had they gathered themselves upon God, they would have had that, and would have obtained with Him the greatest cause.

(p-176) When He had made clear what He had made clear of His dazzling power and His manifest greatness, and had weakened their affair in this world and the Hereafter, and what had preceded had already hinted that they attributed him ﷺ to poetry, and had declared their mockery of the promise, together with what came before that of their denial and of their response to the believers, [namely] their foolishness and their misguidance, He made the following the consequence of that, after having denied them victory, with His words, as consolation to him ﷺ: ﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾. The reading of the majority is with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the zay, and its meaning is "makes [it] in you" (yajʿal fīka). The reading of Nafi' is with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the zay, which indicates that what is forbidden is only excessive grief and being immersed in it, not what arises from the natural disposition of human beings in its origin, for "aḥzana fulānan kadhā" means "he made so-and-so grieved," i.e., made him sorrowful. ﴿Their speech﴾, i.e., what We have already mentioned, by allusion and by explicit statement and otherwise, [directed] at you and at us. And since the Knowing of the Powerful about what His enemy does is a cause for seizing him, He gave the reason for that with His words, threatening with the manifestation of greatness: ﴿Indeed, We know what﴾, i.e., all that, ﴿they conceal﴾, i.e., they renew their concealing of it, ﴿and what they disclose﴾. I.e., We will make what they cause against you a cause for their own harm and for your benefit, until they come into your grasp and under your subjugation and power.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 77:

When He (subhanahu) had established by this proof His power over what He had first threatened with, namely the transformation from one state to another, thereby establishing His power over resurrection (al-ba'th); and when He concluded with the all-encompassing knowledge that necessarily entails the completeness of power, He followed this with a proof clearer than the first. So He said, coordinating it with "Have they not seen" (alam yaraw): ﴿Has he not seen﴾; that is, he knows, with a knowledge that in its clarity is like what is perceived by sight.

Since this parable that this disbeliever uttered would not be approved even by a donkey, were it to speak, He pointed to his dullness by using the expression "the human being" (al-insan), who, although he is the most discerning of created beings with respect to the intellect that He (subhanahu) has placed within him, has been overcome by fondness for himself, to the point that he becomes a parable. So He said: ﴿the human being﴾; that is, the species of him, both among them and among others, although the one concerning whom it was revealed was one person: ﴿that We created him﴾ by the greatness that is ours; ﴿from a drop﴾; that is, a small, insignificant, despicable thing, from water of no benefit, after We originated his father from dust and his mother from flesh and bones; ﴿and behold﴾; that is, as a consequence of Our creating him from that, there is a sudden shift to a state that is farthest of all from the state of a drop, namely that he is ﴿a manifest adversary﴾; that is, one of extreme contention; ﴿clear﴾; that is, in utmost clarity regarding what he desires, to the point that he disputes with the One who gave him intellect and power concerning His power.

The master Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri recited concerning this:

"I teach him archery every day, / but when his forearm grew strong, he shot me."

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 36, verse 78**

[p. 178] Since the implied sense is: "He worshipped, despite Our having singled Him out for bounty, someone other than Us; and he disputed with Our messengers, using the tongue We created for him and the eloquence We gave him, and with all the people of Our love," the next clause follows it, censuring their denial of resurrection with a censure that no one could find more astonishing, more eloquent, or more indicative of persistence in error, excess in denial, and ingratitude for blessings. It reads: ﴿He strikes⁠﻿﻿ ...﻿﻿﻿ ﴾. That is, this human being. The occasion of revelation was Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) killed at Uhud in single combat. He is therefore the one principally and directly intended by this rebuke.

﴿for Us⁠﻿﻿﻿ ﴾, that is, in accordance with what he knows of Our greatness, ﴿a parable⁠﻿﻿﻿ ﴾, that is, his gods which he worshipped, because they are unable to do anything, defying his own intellect in holding that nothing resembles Us.

﴿And he forgets⁠﻿﻿﻿ ﴾, that is, this man who took it upon himself, at the extreme of his origin, to dispute with the Almighty and exposed his face to argue with Him. The word "forgetting" here may carry the sense of heedlessness or the sense of abandonment.

﴿his creation⁠﻿﻿﻿ ﴾, that is, Our creation of this disputant, which indicates the perfection of Our power and that the gods he associated with Him are unable to do anything. Thus the state that the parable had joined together diverged in the most extreme way, and both became addressed as: "O you of little understanding! Is He who creates like He who creates nothing? Will you not then remember?"

Then he continues the report about this parable by reporting its impossibility, [p. 179] namely that anyone should be able to give life to the dead, just as his objects of worship are unable to do so. So He says: ﴿He says⁠﻿﻿﻿ ﴾, that is, by way of denial: ﴿"Who will give life⁠﻿﻿﻿ ...﻿﻿﻿ ﴾.

Since bones are the hardest of things and the furthest from accepting life, especially when they have decayed and crumbled, He says: ﴿the bones, while they are﻿﻿﻿ ﴾. Since He reports about a feminine plural noun by a name for decayed bones which is not an adjective, He does not affix the feminine marker ـة (tāʼ marbūṭah). So He says: ﴿decayed⁠﻿﻿﻿ ﴾, that is, they have become dust carried away by the winds.

When the setting was one in which the listener of this discourse longs for its answer, He resumed His speech, addressing one who does not fully grasp this disputation other than Himself: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to this man who coined this parable out of ignorance, in his analogy of One who has power over everything to one who has power over nothing. He repeated the verb "give life" explicitly to indicate the intended meaning, to repel obstinacy, and to show emphasis, saying: ﴿He who brings them to life﴾, that is, after they have decayed a second time. He turned the statement to a description that points to the judgment, saying: ﴿who produced them﴾, that is, from nothing, ﴿then brought them to life the first time﴾. That is, whoever is able to bring a thing into existence the first time is able to restore it a second time. This is attested by the fact that life inheres in the bone, so that it becomes impure through death, which is why the carcass of a dead creature is judged impure. ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾, that is, every making and every decree. It is possible for Him to create from that and from other than it, both in origination and in restoration. ﴿Knowing﴾, that is, of perfect knowledge, so that nothing of a dead person escapes Him at all, even if its parts are scattered over land and sea, and nothing else is hidden from Him.

The verse is an instance of the wondrous rhetorical device of *ihtibak* (a figure in which two corresponding elements are mentioned, each one's counterpart being left implicit in the other). "Giving life" first implies its like second, and "producing" second implies its like first. And "the first time" in the second half implies "a second time" in the first half. Thus He is "over everything competent," as He demonstrated in Surat Ta-Ha. He brings into being the requisites of every possible thing He wills, removes the obstacles, and so it comes into existence at once, without any delay at all. This explanation, in proving the resurrection both of the body and of the spirit together, has reached the limit beyond which there is no further explanation. It had already prepared the ground for this in this very surah, with what admits of no objection, in His words: ﴿Then, behold, from the graves they will hasten to their Lord﴾ [Ya-Sin: 51]; ﴿"Who has raised us from our resting place?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]; ﴿Then, behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾ [Ya-Sin: 53]; ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in joy, reclining﴾ [Ya-Sin: 55]; ﴿"And separate yourselves today, O criminals"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 59]; ﴿"Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 64]; ﴿Today We seal over their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet testify to what they used to earn﴾ [Ya-Sin: 65].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 80:

Since the outcome of this parable, in which denial was directed at the decayed bones (al-rami), was to deem it unlikely that a thing could be distinguished when it has become dust and has mixed with other dust, He (may His holiness be exalted) described Himself as bringing forth that which is most hidden from its opposite, namely the distinguishing of fire from wood in which water is apparent, by the hands of His creatures who are incapable. So He said, repeating the relative pronoun (al-ladhi) to draw attention to the One described, so that one who is alive would call to mind His attributes of perfection and hasten to submit to Him: ﴿Who has made for you﴾, i.e., as a provision and a means of insight, ﴿from the green tree﴾, in which you see water, ﴿fire﴾, by one of you taking two branches, like two siwak sticks, both green, from which water drips, and rubbing the markh (which is male) upon the 'iffar (which is female), so that fire comes out. Abu Hayyan said: And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both: "There is no tree but that in it there is fire, except the 'unnab (jujube)." End quote.

For this reason they said in the well-known proverb: "In every tree there is fire, and the markh and the 'iffar have been extolled." ﴿Then, behold,﴾ i.e., as a consequence of that, your sudden kindling occurs, because you ﴿from it﴾, i.e., from the tree described as green (p-182) itself, ﴿kindle﴾, i.e., you bring about the kindling, and this recurs for you time after time. It is not an illusion or magic, but a firm and clear reality. It seems that he placed the prepositional phrase first because of how much they kindle from it, and so he counted their kindling from other than it as nothing, both because of its magnitude and its rarity.

When this was not burdensome for them, he placed the preposition phrase first, to single it out and to treat everything else as if it did not exist. So He who was able to distinguish fire from water and wood, and who concealed fire within them (fire does not attack wood to burn it, nor does water attack fire to extinguish it), is able to distinguish the dust of bones from the dust of other things, and to breathe the spirit into them, just as He breathed the spirit of fire into wood, which is opposed to it in its watery nature.

Since the implied sense is: "Is not He who is able to do that able to do what He wills, namely reviving the bones and other things?", he joined to it something greater in importance, measuring the lesser by the greater. So He said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ That is, He brought them into existence from nothing and ordained them. ﴿The heavens and the earth﴾ means in their greatness, their vastness, and the great benefits, structures, wonders and marvels in them. He stated the preposition phrase to establish the matter and to affirm the assertion, saying ﴿able﴾, that is, one who possesses a power to which no power is comparable. The meaning of the recitation of Ruways on the authority of Ya'qub, with a yā' vowelled with a fatḥa, the qāf sukūn without an alif, and the rā' with a ḍammah (i.e., yakhluqa, "creates"), is that He renews the attachment of power continuously. ﴿To create﴾: he turned the discourse to the third person, signalling that by this disputation they had become deserving of the utmost anger. So He said ﴿their likes﴾, that is, the likes of these human beings, meaning He will restore them in their very persons, just as you say, "Someone like you does such-and-such", meaning you yourself. He expressed it this way to convey their contemptibility, and that reviving dead bones is more akin to creating anew, though it falls short of origination in that it has an existing material. He used the plural pronoun because it is more indicative of power. Al-Razi said: "Power is an expression for that attribute by which a thing comes into existence, determined by the determination of will and knowledge, corresponding to them both. Although the attributes of God (exalted is He) are too high for the perception of intellectual reflection to grasp, and for linguistic expressions to reach, this is the utmost extent of human power and of the Arabic language."

Since the answer, after the proofs that have passed, was acknowledgment, He, glorified is He, affirmed what follows the negation, indicating that one must hasten to it and may not hesitate about it; whoever hesitates is obstinate, saying: ﴿Yes indeed﴾, that is, He is able to do that; ﴿and He is﴾, in addition to that, that is, being knowing of creation, ﴿the All-Creator﴾, who attains the utmost in this attribute absolutely, in multiplying creation and repeating it with respect to every thing, in what no illusions can encompass and no minds and understandings can grasp. No one has disputed knowledge of particulars once they exist, as they disputed the power to bring some particulars into being. So he suffices with the form fa'īl, and it is said: ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, that is, the one who attains the utmost in knowledge, which is the source of power, so that nothing, universal or particular, is hidden from Him, in the past, the present, or the future, whether witnessed or unseen.

Having established that, He produced His statement, emphasized because of their denial of the power of resurrection: ﴿Indeed, His command﴾; that is, His affair and His state; ﴿when He intends a thing﴾; that is, the bringing into existence of any thing, whether a substance (jawhar) or an accident ('arad), whatever it may be; ﴿is that He says to it, "Be!"﴾; that is, that He wills it. Then He conjoined it to the answer of the condition, according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i with the accusative (ﷺ-less reading) "fa-yakuna" as a conjoined clause, while on the reading of the others with the nominative He began it as a new sentence with His saying: ﴿so it is﴾; that is, without any delay at all, in accordance with what He willed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 36, verse 83:

When this was so, it followed that they should hasten to declare Him (exalted be He) free of the likenesses they had struck for Him. Therefore He said: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾; that is, He is exalted above every trace of deficiency, with a transcendence that your understandings cannot reach the reality of. He turned away from the pronoun to a description that indicates the utmost greatness, saying: ﴿in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of all things﴾; that is, by His power and disposal alone, not by the hand of another. ﴿The dominion (malakut) of all things﴾; that is, His complete sovereignty, and His possession, both outwardly and inwardly.

Since the implied sense was: "from Him you are originated," He joined to it His saying: ﴿and to Him﴾; that is, not to another, whether dust or anything else. He turned the speech to address them, belittling and despising them, and said: ﴿you will be returned﴾; that is, in meaning, in all your affairs, and in sensible reality, through resurrection, so that He may judge between you, placing some in the Fire and some in the Garden. The reading of the majority, with the passive form, draws attention to the utmost of their lowliness, in that the return is by compulsion and by the easiest of matters. The reading of Ya'qub, with the active form, adds that their submission in the return is, because of how easy it is for Him, as though it arose from their own act by their own choice. Thus it is established that He, glory be to Him, is powerful over all things; and it is established with certainty that He is All-Wise; and it is established with certainty that there is no god but Him, and that His speech is wise. It is also established, through the completeness of His power, that He is Forbearing, not hastening to punish anyone. Thus it is established that He sent the messengers to give glad tidings of His reward and warnings of His punishment; and thus it is established that He sent this noble Prophet, by the miracles with which He strengthened him and the clear proofs He manifested through his hand. So the end of the surah returns, with both the message and the raising of the dead, to its beginning, and its joint connects with what it joins in both matters. And Allah is the Guide to what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final place.
